section.title: Prison Officers
section.p: Mr. Hinchliffe: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department how many prison officers who graduated earlier this month from the Newbold prison officer training school expressed a wish to be placed in posts at prisons within the Yorkshire area; and how many were actually placed in posts within Yorkshire.

Mrs. Rumbold: Twenty-one of the 180 officers who completed their training at Newbold Revel on 12 October named an establishment in North, South or West Yorkshire as their first choice. None was posted there, such vacancies as there were being filled by existing officers with longstanding requests for a transfer.

Mr. Hinchliffe: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department when he expects to reply to the letter of 6 August from the Prison Officers Association branch at Her Majesty's prison, Wakefield, regarding staffing levels.

Mrs. Rumbold: The letter concerned a dispute about the staffing of Her Majesty's prison, Wakefield which was resolved at a national disputes meetings on 2 October. In the light of the outcome of that meeting, one of my officials replied to the letter on 18 October.

Mr. Hinchliffe: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department if he will list the prison officer staffing levels agreed under "fresh start" for Her Majesty's prison, Wakefield and the actual number in post for 1 April 1988, 1 April 1989 and 1 April 1990; and what information he has on the reasons for the differences in these figures.

Mrs. Rumbold: Wakefield prison went on to "fresh start" in April 1988. A staffing level of 429 officers, including principal and senior officers and specialists, was set by the regional director. The actual number of officers in post on the dates in question was:
1 April Number of officers
1988 406
1989 426
1990 440

In setting the original staffing level and in determining subsequently the resources to be allocated to Wakefield, the regional director took account of the needs of the establishment relative to the others in his region and of the contribution which it was able too make to the efficiency improvements which were an integral part of the "fresh start" package.

section.title: Lorrain Osman
section.p: Mr. Sheerman: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department how long has Lorrain Osman now been in prison on remand.

Mrs. Rumbold: Mr. Osman was held on remand only from 7 December 1985 until 1 June 1987. On that date he was committed to custody by the chief metropolitan stipendiary magistrate to await the Secretary of State's order for his surrender. The Secretary of State has been prevented from completing his consideration of the extradition request from Hong Kong because of the series of appeals initiated by Mr. Osman, the last of which is outstanding.

section.title: Remand Prisoners
section.p: Mr. Sheerman: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what is the longest time any prisoner has been imprisoned on remand (a) in the last 30 years, (b) in the last 20 years and (c) in the last 10 years.

Mrs. Rumbold: Information about the longest periods held in remand during the last 30 years is not available centrally. On 30 June 1990 one unconvicted prisoner had been held in Pentonville prison for more than four and a half years having been committed to custody pending completion of extradition proceedings. An indication of the length of time spent in prison service establishments by person received on remand is published annually in "Prison Statistics England and Wales"—tables 2.3 and 2.4 of the latest issue, for 1989, Cm. 1221, copies of which are in the Library.

section.title: Ritual Murder (Leaflet)
section.p: Mr. Janner: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what investigations the police are conducting into the identity of those responsible for publication or distribution of the leaflet "Another Blood Libel or Ritual Murder".

Mr. Peter Lloyd: I understand from the Commissioner of Police of the Metropolis that inquiries have established that the names given for the publisher and the printer of the leaflet are false. The investigation is continuing.

section.title: RELATE
section.p: Mr. Mullin: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what financial contributions his Department is making to RELATE; if it plans to increase its contribution; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. John Patten: In the present financial year RELATE will receive a grant of £1,306,840, which includes a special grant of £300,000. I am not yet in a position to say what its grant for the following year will be.

section.title: Birmingham Pub Bombings
section.p: Dr. Kim Howells: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department when he expects the inquiry by the Devon and Cornwall police into the Birmingham pub bombings to be complete; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. John Patten: In the light of new information discovered by the Devon and Cornwall constabulary, my right hon. and learned Friend referred the cases of the Birmingham Six to the Court of Appeal on 29 August. Any further police inquiries into these cases in connection with the hearing before the Court of Appeal are a matter for the Director of Public Prosecutions.

section.title: AIDS (Police Information)
section.p: Mr. Chris Smith: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department whether any information or data are recorded, referenced or retained by the police on their manual files or upon computer, including the national police computer, the Metropolitan police computer and any other constabulary computer, which describes, or can identify, an individual as being antibody positive to a test for human immunodeficiency virus or as having an AIDS 20 diagnosis or any related human immunodeficiency virus illness or which describes that individual as being contagious as a consequence of such diagnosis; whether guidelines have been issued to the police in relation to the recording of such information; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Peter Lloyd: My right hon. and noble Friend the Minister of State, the Earl Ferrers, wrote to the hon. Member on 16 October on these matters. As he explained in the letter, it is for chief officers to decide what information to keep on local force computers and manual records. He also confirmed that police forces are able to record on the police national computer information on the health or likely behaviour of a person where such information would be of help to them in dealing with that person. The reply to a question by the hon. Member for Denton and Reddish (Mr. Bennett) on 15 October at column 725, sets out the warning signals which may be used on the police national computer. These include a warning that the subject of the record may be a hazard to others as a carrier of diseases. It is for the police to decide whether to use this or any other warning signal.

section.title: Green Issues
section.p: Mr. Flynn: To ask the Prime Minister what benefits Her Majesty's Government gained from the attendance by an official of her efficiency unit at the Royal Institute for Public Administration conference on greening the way we govern at Royal Holloway college on 21–22 September.

The Prime Minister: I understand that a member of the efficiency unit accepted a personal invitation to chair a session on "Environment, accountability and value for money". No costs were incurred by Government.

section.title: Romanian Children
section.p: Mr. Flynn: To ask the Prime Minister what initiative she put forward to support Romanian children suffering from AIDS and other diseases during her visit to the United Nations conference on children in New York in September.

The Prime Minister: At the world summit for children. I signed the world declaration on the survival, protection and development of children and supported the plan of action. Both documents recognised the urgent need to accord a high priority to health care and to AIDS programmes for children in all countries, including Romania.

section.title: Statutory Instruments
section.p: Mr. Robin Maxwell-Hyslop: To ask the Prime Minister whether she will include in the Official Report a table showing, for each of the last 10 Sessions, the ratio of statutory instruments introduced by the negative resolution procedure to those by the affirmative resolution procedure.

The Prime Minister: Figures for the numbers of statutory instruments laid before the House each Session are not readily available. However, all instruments laid, with the exception of Orders in Council and draft Orders
21 in Council made or proposed to be made under paragraph 1 of schedule 1 to the Northern Ireland Act 1974, are considered by the Joint or Select Committee on Statutory Instruments. The following figures, derived from the sessional returns relating the delegated legislation, are based on instruments considered by these Committees during each of the last 10 full Sessions. Excluded from the figures are statutory rules of Northern Ireland, special procedure orders and all instruments which are not subject to parliamentary procedure.

td.i: Instruments considered by the Joint or Select Committee on Statutory Instruments

section.title: Leaks
section.p: Mr. Campbell-Savours: To ask the Prime Minister (1) how many persons elected to the office of Member of Parliament, office holders and non-office holders, other than the Chancellor of the Exchequer and the Prime Minister knew, prior to 4 pm on Friday 5 October, of the Chancellor of the Exchequer's intention to announce in October either a cut in base rates or entry into the exchange rate mechanism;

(2) whether she will institute a full leak inquiry into how information relating to the cut in base rates and exchange rate mechanism entry was known to individuals in the City of London more than one and a half hours prior to the statement by the Chancellor of the Exchequer at 4 pm on Friday 5 October;

(3) how many civil servants knew prior to 4 pm on Friday 5 October of the Chancellor of the Exchequer's intention to announce in October either a cut in base rate or entry into the exchange rate mechanism.

The Prime Minister: Only those with an operational need to know were informed prior to 4 pm on Friday 5 October of the Chancellor of the Exchequer's intention to announce a cut in base rates and the Government's decision to enter the exchange rate mechanism on Monday 8 October.

I have no evidence to suggest that information relating to the cut in base rates and entry in to the exchange rate mechanism was known to anyone in the City of London outside the Bank of England prior to the Chancellor of the Exchequer's statement. If the hon. Gentleman believes that he has such evidence he should make it available to the appropriate authorities.

section.title: Foreign Troops (Training)
section.p: Mr. O'Neill: To ask the Prime Minister which Government Department is responsible for granting approval to companies seeking to provide military 22 training for foreign military forces when such training involves the release of United Kingdom classified information.
The Prime Minister: Were any such requests for approval to be made, they would be considered by the Department or Departments which had originated the United Kingdom classified information concerned.

section.title: European Bank for Reconstruction and Development
section.p: Mr. Tredinnick: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs when he expects the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development to open; what discussions he has had concerning the bank recently; and if he will make a statement.

Mrs. Chalker: The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development will be able to start operations when so authorised by the inaugural meeting of its board of governors. This will be held when the bank's articles of agreement have been ratified by members with two thirds of the total voting power, to include at least two borrowing members. The ratification process is likely to be concluded by next spring.

I opened the second conference of prospective members of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development at Lancaster house today which will review progress in developing a sound operational framework for the new bank. I am confident that the bank will soon be able to play its part in fostering private enterprise and economic development in central and eastern European countries committed to democratic principles and market economics.

section.title: Cambodia
section.p: Mr. Cryer: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs if he will list for 1988, 1989 and 1990 to the most recent practicable date the development aid given to Cambodia by the United Kingdom Government; and if he will make a statement.

Mrs. Chalker: I refer the hon. Member to the answer I gave to my hon. Friend the Member for Broxtowe (Mr. Lester) on 15 October, at column 633. Britain has no Government-to-Government aid programme in Cambodia, but details of humanitarian aid provided to Cambodians since 1988–89 is as follows:

section.p: Mrs. Mahon: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs for what reason a proposal for the repair of a water filtration plant in Cambodia was turned down.

Mrs. Chalker: Oxfam applied in 1988 for co-funding of a water distribution project in Phnom Penh under our joint funding scheme. When we told non-governmental organisations, including Oxfam, that we were prepared to support projects in Cambodia, we indicated that we would prefer to consider smaller-scale development projects with a humanitarian element and not infrastructural projects concerned with restoring or maintaining major public utilities which are more usually the concern of government rather than non-governmental organisations.

This project fell into that second category and was therefore rejected. Since 1988–89 we have committed £565,000 to co-fund 12 projects in Cambodia carried out by non-governmental organisations, including five from Oxfam, and are currently considering five new proposals, including three from Oxfam.

section.title: Developing Countries (Conference)
section.p: Mr. Flynn: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs what contribution his Department made to the 11th review conference of CAB 24 International on technological assistance and ecological protection in developing countries, held in London at the end of July.

Mrs. Chalker: I gave the opening address at CAB International's 11th review conference. My Department represented the dependent territories at the conference and one of my senior officials was a member of the United Kingdom delegation. Following the conference we are considering with CAB International possible forms of assistance during its transition to a more commercial footing. My Department was also represented at CAB International's workshop on the ecological foundations of sustainable agriculture which was held a few days before the review conference.

section.title: Brazil
section.p: Mr. Flynn: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs what discussions he or officials in his Department have had with Ministers or officials of the Brazilian Government in regard to technical and planning assistance available from the United Kingdom to support RIMA environment impact studies, in particular on the development of ecologically balanced projects in the Amazonian rain forests.

Mrs. Chalker: There have been discussions between officials about assistance for training in environmental impact assessment. A proposal for British support for a joint review of Brazil's environmental impact assessment needs is at a preliminary planning stage and requires detailed discussions with the Brazilian Government. All project proposals for British support in Brazil are of course assessed for their likely environmental impact. Under our bilateral programmes we can support Brazilians to undertake in the United Kingdom training in environmental assessment techniques.

section.title: South America
section.p: Dr. Kim Howells: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs if the Government have plans to discuss further the rescheduling of the external debts of those countries in South America which are currently allocating significant resources to the task of preserving remaining areas of natural rain forest.
Mrs. Chalker: The Government recognise that many of those countries in South America with large areas of rain forest face serious debt problems.
The Paris club is always ready to discuss, where necessary, the rescheduling of official debt for countries pursuing IMF-agreed economic reform programmes.

Much of the South American countries' debt belongs to commercial banks: arrangements for dealing with this debt are a matter for negotiation between the debtor countries and the banks within the framework of the strengthened debt strategy.

section.title: Pergau Hydro-electric Project
section.p: Mrs. Clwyd: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs how much aid has been offered under the aid and trade provision to support contracts between the Malaysian Government and Balfour Beatty, General Electric Company, and Trafalgar House for the Pergau hydro-electric project.

Mrs. Chalker: An offer of a grant of up to £68·25 million from the aid and trade provision, based on an estimated contract value of £316 million, was made on 17 April 1989. An extension of this offer expired on 17 October 1990. A further extension remains a possibility, but no decisions have been taken.

section.title: Lorries (Magor and Undy)
section.p: Mr. Roy Hughes: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales what action he proposes concerning the petition from the No Lorries Through Magor and Undy Action Group presented at the Welsh Office, Cardiff on Friday 12 October.
Sir Wyn Roberts: The petition is being taken into account in the consideration of construction traffic routes in Gwent.

section.title: Young People (Secure Accommodation)
section.p: Mr. Michael: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales (1) if he will list for each local social services authority in Wales for each of the years 1975, 1980, 1985, 1987, 1988 and 1989 the number of placements made in facilities providing secure accommodation and indicate what proportion of those children in the care of the home authority such a number represents;

(2) if he will list for each facility in Wales providing secure accommodation for young persons for each of the years 1975, 1980, 1985, 1987, 1988 and 1989 the number and proportion of young persons so accommodated on behalf of a local social services authority other than that providing the secure accommodation.
Mr. Grist: I refer the hon. Gentleman to the answer I gave on Thursday 18 October.

section.title: Infertility
section.p: Mr. Wigley: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales if he will publish the most recent figures available showing the number of clinics in Wales offering (a) IVA, GIFT arid other procedures and (b) GIFT and other procedures but excluding IVA; and if he will also publish the total numbers of (i) single, (ii) twin, (iii) triplet, (iv) quadruplet, (v) quintuplet and (vi) sextuplet pregnancies following GIFT procedures in each category of clinic.

Mr. Grist: The information requested is not available centrally. However, some information on these matters is published in the annual report of the Interim Licensing Authority, a copy of which is available in the Library. The Interim Licensing Authority was established by the Medical Research Council and the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists in 1985.

It is expected that in future some of the data requested will be available from the IVF register, which has been set up by the Office of Population Censuses and Surveys with funding from the Department.

section.title: European Regional Development Fund
section.p: Mr. Win Griffiths: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales if he will list the annual sums of money committed since the inception of the European regional development fund to each recipient local authority and the annual amount paid to each from the fund.
Mr. David Hunt: The information requested is not readily available and could be provided only at disproportionate cost.

section.title: Childbirth Statistics
section.p: Mr. Wigley: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales if he will publish figures for 1988 and 1989 showing the estimated percentage of women delivering in Wales (a) whose labours were induced, (b) whose labours were of spontaneous onset and (c) who had elective caesarean section.
Mr. Grist: The available information is given in the table. Information for 1989 is not yet available.

section.title: Sewage
section.p: Mr. Michael: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales what consideration he has given to setting special requirements in respect of the treatment of sewage from hospitals in Wales in general and particularly in regard to Ysbyty Gwynedd; what factors were taken into account; and what conclusions were reached.
Mr. Grist: Under the Water Act 1989, the setting of discharge consents is a matter for the National Rivers Authority.

section.title: Rents to Mortgages
section.p: Mr. Morgan: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales how many sales have been completed under the rents to mortgages scheme.

Mr. Grist: Out of some 60 applications, 10 sales have been completed under the flexi-ownership scheme. The Development Board for Rural Wales estimates that by the end of the first year of the scheme about 5 per cent. of the eligible stock will have been sold to flexi-owners.

section.title: Grant-maintained Schools
section.p: Dr. Kim Howells: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales how many applications have been received by his Department from schools wishing to opt out of local authority control in order to attain grant-maintained status.
Sir Wyn Roberts: Two.

section.title: Cot Deaths
section.p: Mr. Alex Carlile: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales how many deaths by sudden infant death syndrome were recorded in Wales in each of the years 1980 to 1989; and if he will make a statement as to measures which he proposes to take to reduce the incidence of sudden infant death syndrome in Wales.

Mr. Grist: Recommendations to secure improvements in the quality of care for new-born babies and their mothers, including the establishment of a regional perinatal intensive care service and a regional paediatric pathology service at University hospital of Wales—UHW—Cardiff, were made in the perinatal mortality initiative report in 1986. Subsequently, the Secretary of State decided that an expert advisory group would be set up to consider the operational structure of the proposed regional centre and its relationship to other perinatal services in Wales. That group, chaired by Sir Eric Stroud, professor of child health at Kings College school of medicine and dentistry, produced a report "Perinatal Intensive Care Services in Wales", which was widely distributed to interested authorities and professional bodies in Wales in February this year.

The report makes a number of recommendations for the improvement of services and identifies in detail the manpower and other requirements for the development of the regional centre at UHW which will be associated with a number of regional sub-centres strategically located throughout the Principality.

Action has been put in hand to secure, by central funding, the appointment of a consultant paediatric pathologist for the regional centre at UHW. Pending this appointment part-time consultant sessions are being funded centrally. Funds are also to be made available to South Glamorgan health authority in the coming financial year to secure the services of a consultant neonatologist and a registrar in paediatrics in line with the recommendations of the report. It is also intended to establish, over the coming five-year period, a programme of developments which will lead to the provision of an integrated service of excellence. As the first stage, health authorities have been asked to prepare proposals to achieve a rationalisation of services in relation to the numbers of special care costs and neo-natal intensive care costs which the report considers necessary to meet the needs in those areas.

section.title: Hospice Movement
section.p: Mr. Ieuan Wyn Jones: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales when he intends to announce the level of funding for the hospice movement in Wales.
Mr. Grist: An announcement will be made as soon as possible.

section.title: Haemophiliacs
section.p: Sir David Steel: To ask the Secretary of State for Health if, in light of the remarks made by Mr. Justice Ognall, he will reconsider his position on compensating haemophiliac HIV sufferers who contracted the disease by way of contaminated blood products.

Mrs. Virginia Bottomley: I refer the right hon. Member to the reply my right hon. and learned Friend the Secretary of State gave the right hon. Member for Manchester, Wythenshawe (Mr. Morris) on 15 October at columns 664–66.

Mr. Allen: To ask the Secretary of State for Health what is the annual cost to the National Health Service in the Nottingham district health authority for staff who have been employed through agencies as nurses, operating department assistants, ancilliary and other staff.

Mrs. Virginia Bottomley: Nottingham health authority has provided the following breakdown of costs to the health authority for non-NHS (agency) staff:

section.title: Alternative Therapies
section.p: Mr. Atkinson: To ask the Secretary of State for Health if he has any plans to recompense qualified medical practitioners using alternative therapies under the National Health Service; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Dorrell: There are no such plans. Registered medical practitioners may, within the services they provide to NHS patients, offer to use any of the complementary therapies if they consider it to be in the interests of their patients.

section.title: Physiotherapy
section.p: Mr. Robin Cook: To ask the Secretary of State for Health what was the number of places available annually for training students in physiotherapy in each of the last 10 years; and what assessment he has made of the adequacy of the number of existing places.

Mrs. Virginia Bottomley: Information on the number of pre-registration training places for physiotherapists was not collected before 1986. The available figures are for Great Britain and are as follows:
Year Number
1986 987
1987 970
1988 994
1989 1,048

The responsibility for ensuring an adequate supply of training places is a matter for regional health authorities in consultation with units providing a service. Guidance has been issued which clearly places a responsibility on regional health authorities to assess demand for training and to ensure that training places are available to meet such a demand.

section.title: Air Ambulances
section.p: Mr. Moate: To ask the Secretary of State for Health which hospital regions of the United Kingdom have the use of air ambulances; what is the basis of funding this service; and if he will institute a study into the possible provision of such a service on a nationwide basis.

Mr. Dorrell: This information is not collected centrally. A study is being carried out into the services in two areas and the results will be considered in due course. The services provided in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland are the responsibility of my right hon. and learned Friend the Secretary of State for Scotland and my right hon. Friends the Secretaries of State for Wales and for Northern Ireland.

section.title: Residential Homes
section.p: 198. Mr. David Nicholson: To ask the Secretary of State for Health whether he will introduce guidelines indicating the attitude local authority social services departments should take over the size, unit bed limits and staffing of registered care homes.
Mrs. Virginia Bottomley: There are no plans to do so at present. "Home Life"—a code of practice for residential care—already gives general guidance on such matters.

199. Mr. David Nicholson: To ask the Secretary of State for Health what representations he has received protesting at the interpretation of the provisions in the Registered Homes Act 1984 regarding unit size and bed limits by certain local authority social services departments.
Mrs. Virginia Bottomley: A small number of letters about this has been received in the Department.

section.title: Baby Milk
section.p: Mr. Fearn: To ask the Secretary of State for Health if midwives are regarded as one of the groups of relevant health professionals which should be consulted by district health authorities about the purchase of baby milk formulas.
Mrs. Virginia Bottomley: Midwives, because of their key role in the provision of maternity care, should be among the health care professionals from whom advice is sought.

Mr. Fearn: To ask the Secretary of State for Health what assessment he has made of the problems which could arise from purchasing baby milk from only one manufacturer; and what guidance he has given to health authorities.
Mrs. Virginia Bottomley: All supplies personnel are aware of the problems that may arise by purchasing any vital product from only one manufacturer.

section.title: Junior Doctors
section.p: Mr. Cryer: To ask the Secretary of State for Health if he intends to introduce legislation to limit the working week of junior doctors to 72 hours; or to recommend such a maximum; and if he will make a statement.
Mrs. Virginia Bottomley: The group on junior doctors' hours, which I chair, is considering a variety of changes in working practices in order to reduce onerous hours of work.
All parties on the ministerial group are aiming to reach broad agreement in principle on specific changes by the end of the year.
The Government have accepted an average 72-hour week for junior hospital doctors as a sensible long-term objective.

section.title: Secure Accommodation
section.p: Mr. Michael: To ask the Secretary of State for Health if he will list for each facility providing secure accommodation for young persons for each of the years 1975, 1980, 1985, 1987, 1988 and 1989, and the number and proportion of young persons so accommodated on behalf of a local social services authority other than that providing the secure accommodation.
Mrs. Virginia Bottomley: I refer the hon. Member to the reply I gave him on 18 October at column 891.

Mr. Michael: To ask the Secretary of State for Health if he will list for each local social services authority for each of the years 1975, 1980, 1985, 1987, 1988 and 1989 the number of placements made in facilities providing secure accommodation; and what proportion of those children in the care of the home authority such a number represents.

Mrs. Virginia Bottomley: The number of placements made in facilities providing secure accommodation for the years 1985 to 1988 is published in "Children accommodated in secure units during the year ended 31 March", copies of which are available in the Library. Figures for 1989 will be available shortly. This information was not collected centrally prior to 1985. Figures on proportions could be obtained only at disproportionate cost.

section.title: Adoption
section.p: Mr. Harry Barnes: To ask the Secretary of State for Health when he intends to issue a report on adoption procedures; which categories of people have and will be consulted in the process of drawing up the report; and whether procedures for adoption of children from Romania are under consideration.

Mrs. Virginia Bottomley: Three discussion papers were issued in September in connection with the interdepartmental review of adoption law. The papers have been circulated widely for comment among groups and individuals with an interest in adoption; and are freely available to all interested parties. Further papers in the series will follow, including a discussion paper on inter-country adoption.
New guidance was issued in September to social services departments on inter-country adoption, including adoption of Romanian children.
Copies of the adoption law review papers and of the guidance on inter-country adoption have been placed in the Library.

section.title: Incontinence Pads
section.p: Mr. Harry Barnes: To ask the Secretary of State for Health (1) if he will list district health authorities in England and Wales, showing which of these charge private residential nursing homes for the use of incontinence pads for national health service patients who are their residents;

(2) how many representations he has received in the current year concerning district health authorities charging private residential nursing homes for incontinence pads for national health service patients who are their residents and if he will make a statement.

(3) if he will list the standard charges by district health authorities to private residential nursing homes for the use of incontinence pads for national health service patients who are their residents.

Mr. Dorrell: We have received a number of representations about the supply of incontinence pads to private nursing and residential homes. The free provision of incontinence pads under the National Health Service Act 1977 does not extend to people living in private nursing homes; the same legislation provides that district health authorities may provide incontinence materials and other nursing aids to people in their own homes and at their discretion to residents of local authority and private residential homes. The extent to which this discretion is exercised varies from place to place and information about these decisions is not held centrally.

section.title: Infertility Treatments
section.p:
Mr. Wigley: To ask the Secretary of State for Health if he will publish the most recent figures available showing the number of clinics in (a) England and (b) England and
33 Wales offering (i) IVF, GIFT and other procedures and (ii) GIFT and other procedures but excluding IVF; and if he will also publish the total numbers of (a) single, (b) twin, (c) triplet, (d) quadruplet, (e) quintuplet and (f) sextuplet pregnancies following GIFT procedures in each category of clinic.

Mrs. Virginia Bottomley: The information requested is not available centrally. Some information on these matters is published in the annual report of the Interim Licensing Authority, a copy of which is available in the Library.
In future we expect that some of the data requested will be available from the IVF register, which has been set up by OPCS with funding from the Department.

section.p: Mr. Wigley: To ask the Secretary of State for Health if he will publish the most recent figures available showing the estimated percentage of women delivering in (a) England and (b) England and Wales (i) whose labours were induced, (ii) whose labours were of spontaneous onset and (iii) who had elective Caesarean section.

section.title: Wakefield Health Authority
section.p: Mr. Hinchliffe: To ask the Secretary of State for Health what are the names, home addresses, ages and occupations of the newly appointed chairman, executive and non-executive members of Wakefield health authority

Mrs. Virginia Bottomley: Brian Hayward was appointed the chairman of Wakefield health authority 34 from 14 November 1988 until 31 March 1992. The hon. Member may care to write to Mr. Hayward at the district health authority for his personal details.

The Yorkshire regional health authority is responsible for appointing the non-executive members of Wakefield health authority. The chief officer and the chief finance officer are "ex-officio" executive members of the authority. Other executives are appointed by the chairman, the non-executives and the chief officer.
The hon. Member may therefore wish to contact Sir Bryan Askew, chairman of Yorkshire regional health authority, for the information he requires.

section.title: Acute Care
section.p: Dr. Kim Howells: To ask the Secretary of State for Health what guidelines are issued by his Department to area health authorities as to the relative priority to he granted to patients (a) over the age of 70 years and (b) under the age of 70 years who have been diagnosed as having suffered serious coronary attacks, in respect of acute care treatments.
Mrs. Virginia Bottomley: None. The treatment of an individual patient is a matter for the clinician responsible for his or her care.

section.title: General Practitioners
section.p: Mr. Michael Morris: To ask the Secretary of State for Health whether he has any plans to allow general practitioners a statutory right to buy their premises where they are owned by the public sector.

Mrs. Virginia Bottomley: Health authorities are at liberty to sell unneeded health centres to general practitioners, provided suitable arrangements are made for the continuing provision of any community services based there.

Mr. Michael Morris: To ask the Secretary of State for Health if, further to his answer of 16 October. Official Report, column 1045, he will publish the evidence showing that the amount of time general practitioners spend with patients is increasing.

Mrs. Virginia Bottomley: My right hon. and learned Friend the Secretary of State's comments were based on a survey published in "PULSE" on 4 August, which showed 54 per cent. of GPs had spent more time in patient contact since the inception of the new contract. A copy of this publication is available in the Library.

section.title: Eye Tests
section.p: Mr. Tony Banks: To ask the Secretary of State for Health what information he has on the impact of charging to for eyesight checks on attendances for examination in the London borough of Newham.

Mrs. Virginia Bottomley: Information about NHS sight tests is not collected for individual London boroughs. Figures are available, however, for regional health authorities. For North East Thames regional health authority, which includes the London borough of Newham, the number of NHS sight tests paid for in 1988–89 and 1989–90 by family health service authorities in that region was as follows:
NHS Sight Tests
35
1988–89: 1,054,960
1989–90 (after entitlement was restricted to certain groups): 468,230.
After 1 April 1989, many patients in Newham, as elsewhere, will have had a private eye examination. Regular statistics are not kept on private sight tests.

section.title: NHS Capital Programme
section.p: Mr. Michael Morris: To ask the Secretary of State for health what report the national health service management board has made to him on the impact on the capital programme of the national health service arising from the fall in property values.
Mr. Dorrell: None.

section.title: Bed Closures
section.p: Mr. Michael Morris: To ask the Secretary of State for Health with what frequency he requires the national health service management board to report on the number of bed closures by region or district; and what are the latest figures.
Mr. Dorrell: We do not require reports from the management executive on numbers of bed closures since this information is not an accurate guide to the level of services to patients.

section.title: Heracleum Mantegazzianum
section.p: Mrs. Margaret Ewing: To ask the Secretary of State for Health how many recorded incidents there have been in the last five years of the hospitalisation of patients who have come into contact with the furocoumarins released by heracleum mantegazzianum
Mr. Dorrell: This information is not available.

section.title: Hostels
section.p: Mr. Kirkwood: To ask the Secretary of State for Health whether he will give social services departments overall responsibility for financing the cost of care in hostels to the extent that it is not covered by other existing funding; and if he will make a statement.

Mrs. Virginia Bottomley: Local authorities have powers under existing legislation to support hostels and the people in them. It is for each local authority to decide the type and level of support to make available.

section.title: Vitamin A Supplements
section.p: Mr. Michael Morris: To ask the Secretary of State for Health if he will identify the research or peer review journal which led to his Department's decision to recommend restricted consumption of liver and vitamin A supplements; and whether he has any plans to make the findings of this research more widely available.

Mr. Dorrell: A number of pieces of research contributed to the Department's decision. The major contributing factor was the increasing knowledge of the potential teratogenicity of vitamin A and growing evidence that the consumption of high amounts of vitamin A by pregnant women may be associated with birth defects in their babies. This information is reviewed in the following publications: Rosa FW, Wilk AL and Kelsey 36 FO (1986) Teratology 33, 355–364; Biesalski HK (1989) Toxicology 57, 117–161 and Teratology Society position paper: "Recommendations for Vitamin A use during pregnancy" (1987) Teratology 35 269–275. Results of recent measurements of vitamin A levels in samples of domestic and imported liver on sale in the United Kingdom are quoted in the Department's press release of 18 October 1990, ref 90/507. Copies of these documents have been placed in the Library.

section.title: Electromagnetic Fields
section.p: Mr. Simon Hughes: To ask the Secretary of State for Health if he will list the research projects he has instigated into the potential health implications resulting from exposure to electromagnetic fields.

Mr. Dorrell [holding answer 19 October 1990]: The National Radiological Protection Board is under a statutory duty to inform and advise Government and others on possible hazards to health from ionising and non-ionising radiation. The board has undertaken an extensive review of the possible health consequences of exposure to electromagnetic fields. The review, to be published shortly, will form the basis of a revision of the board's recommendations published in 1989 entitled, "Guidance on Exposure to Time-Varying Electromagnetic Fields" (NRPB-GS11), a copy of which is in the Library.

Projects undertaken by board staff include measurement of occupational and domestic electromagnetic fields and theoretical calculation of energy absorption in people. A programme of work investigating the cancer-related responses of cell cultures to electromagnetic fields is to begin shortly.

section.title: Industrial Deafness
section.p: Mr. Rowlands: To ask the Secretary of State for Health whether he will list the type of machines covered by provisions relating to industrial deafness; when that list was compiled; when it was last revised; and whether he will review the list.

Mr. Scott: I have been asked to reply. The machines specified in the jobs prescribed for occupational deafness are listed in schedule 1, part 1, of the Social Security (Industrial Injuries) (Prescribed Diseases) Regulations 1985 as amended by regulation 2 of the Social Security (Industrial Injuries) (Prescribed Diseases) Amendment (No. 2) Regulations 1987. The list can also be found in leaflet NI 207 "If you think your job has made you deaf—copies of which are available in the Library. The list was first prescribed in 1975 and last revised in 1988. The Industrial Injuries Advisory Council reviewed the list in Cm. 817 "Occupational Deafness"—October 1989—but decisions on its recommendations were deferred pending a further report from the council on improving the administrative arrangements for dealing with claims for this disease. This report will be published very shortly. The council has asked the Department to evaluate the feasibility of the report's recommendations within six months. It should then be easier to determine whether there are orderly ways in which to extend provision for this disease to further occupations.

section.title: Planning Applications (London)
