section.title: Electoral Statistics
section.p: Mr. Maxwell-Hyslop: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department whether he will publish in the Official Report the tables given in paragraphs 45 and 46 of the Home Office memorandum submitted to the Home Affairs Committee in connection with its report intituled "Redistribution of Seats" (second report Session 1986–87), revised in respect of the latest available figures, showing the total numbers of electors in England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

Mrs. Rumbold: The information requested, based on figures for the 1990 electorate, is given in the tables. The tables illustrate two different ways in which equal standards of parliamentary representation throughout the United Kingdom might be achieved, by the introduction of a single electoral quota for the United Kingdom. Table 1 is based on a total of 650 seats; table 2 is based on a total of 799 seats, maintaining the present number of seats in Scotland.

section.title: Police Personnel
section.p: Mr. Trotter: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what is the ratio of police personnel to the population in the United Kingdom; and what is the comparable figure for the other countries of the European Community.

Mr. Peter Lloyd: My right hon. and learned Friend is responsible for policing in England and Wales where the police population ratio was 1:404 as at 31 December 1989. Ratios for other European Community countries are not held centrally although the Home Affairs Committee (seventh report volume I table II) published relevant information about population and police numbers. In comparing one country with another one must, of course, have regard to a variety of matters including the responsibilities of particular police organisations and the policing style which is adopted.

section.title: Northumbria Probation Service
section.p: Ms. Quin: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what additional resources have been made available to the Northumbria probation service as a result of the extra demand caused by the dispersal of prisoners following events at Strangeways prison in April 1990.

Mr. John Patten: Chief probation officers in the north of England, including Northumbria, were notified in July of action they should take to deal with this problem. They were advised that if the extra necessary resources could not be found locally, the Home Office would consider the funding of temporary additions to staffing levels. No such applications have been received.

section.title: Northumbria Police Authority
section.p: Ms. Quin: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what additional resources have been provided by his Department to the Northumbria police authority to meet the extra demands caused by dispersal of prisoners following events at Strangeways prison in April 1990.

Mr. Peter Lloyd: Police authorities are able to claim the reimbursement of certain extra costs incurred by the police in undertaking tasks which would normally be carried out by the prison service. No such claim has yet been received from the Northumbria police authority.

Ms. Quin: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department (1) if his Department will provide figures for each month from May 1990 onwards for the number of remand prisoners and newly sentenced prisoners being held in the police cells in Northumbria police authority area who would normally be housed in Strangeways or Armley prisons;

(2) if his Department will provide figures for each month from May 1990 onwards for the number of remand prisoners formerly imprisoned in Strangeways prison, Manchester, who are now being held in police cells in the Northumbria police authority area.

Mrs. Rumbold: The average numbers of convicted and unconvicted prisoners, who have been held in police cells in the Northumbria police authority area each month since May 1990, are given in the table. All would normally have been held in Strangeways.
This information is not collected in a way that enables the number of newly sentenced prisoners or those held in Strangeways before the April riot to be readily identified separately.

section.title: Correspondence
section.p: Mr. Kaufman: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department (1) when he intends to reply to the letters to him dated 2 May, 25 June and 2 August from the right hon. Member for Manchester, Gorton with regard to Mr. and Mrs. V. Stringer, 18 Underwood close, Mr. and Mrs. E. Iddon, Walesside house and Mr. and Mrs. R. Graham, 1 Falmer close;
(2) when he intends to reply to the letters to him dated 30 April, 25 June and 2 August from the right hon. Member for Manchester, Gorton with regard to Mrs. I. Neill, 6 Calverley avenue.
Mr. Mellor: I have been asked to reply.

I regret that these letters went astray within the Home Office. The right hon. Member for Manchester, Gorton has already forwarded to me a copy of his letter of 30 April on behalf of Mrs. I. Neill, and I have replied to him today. If he would make available copies of the other correspondence I will ensure he receives responses straight away.

section.title: Football (Arrests)
section.p: Mr. Tony Banks: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what information he has regarding the number of arrests inside London football grounds this season.
Mr. Peter Lloyd: Arrest figures for Football League matches will not be collated until the end of the season.

section.title: Prevention of Terrorism
section.p: Mr. Mills: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department how observations from interested persons or organisations should be submitted for consideration by Lord Colville in his report on the operation in 1990 of the Prevention of Terrorism (Temporary Provisions) Act 1989.
Mr. Waddington: Written observations should be submitted to Lord Colville, c/o Room 647, Home Office, 50 Queen Anne's Gate, London SW1H 9AT no later than Friday 21 December 1990.

section.title: Harmondsworth Detention Centre
section.p: Mr. Mills: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department whether he has yet established an independent body to monitor the welfare of detainees and to advise on the running of Harmondsworth detention centre, as recommended by Her Majesty's chief inspector of prisons.

Mr. Waddington: I have appointed 11 members to this body, which is to be known as the Harmondsworth visiting committee. Its inaugural meeting took place on 25 September 1990. I am confident that the committee is well equipped to represent the interests of detainees at Harmondsworth.

section.title: Shipstones Brewery, Nottingham
section.p: Mr. Allen: To ask the Secretary of State for Trade and Industry if he will meet the chair of Greenall Whitney Brewers to discuss the closure of the Shipstones brewery in Nottingham; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Douglas Hogg: The Secretary of State has not received an invitation to meet the chairman of Greenall Whitley Plc, and will not be seeking such a meeting. Any decision to cease production at the Shipstones brewery in Nottingham and in Warrington is one for the commercial judgment of the company.

section.title: Information Technology
section.p: 218. Mr. Ron Brown: To ask the Secretary of State for Trade and Industry what representations he has received about the future of the British information technology industry.
Mr. Douglas Hogg: My Department regularly receives representations about many areas of industry, including the IT sector.

section.title: Cash Flow Statements
section.p: 210. Mr. Austin Mitchell: To ask the Secretary of State for Trade and Industry whether he will seek to amend the Companies Acts to require all public limited companies to publish a cash flow statement.

Mr. Redwood: No. In July 1990, the Accounting Standards Committee issued an exposure draft proposing that the statement of source and applications of funds which is presently required by "Statement of Standard Accounting Practice 10" should be replaced by a statement of cash flow. I understand that the Accounting Standards Board will be taking up this issue when the period allowed for comment on the exposure draft has expired.

section.title: Accountancy Bodies
section.p: 216. Mr. Austin Mitchell: To ask the Secretary of State for Trade and Industry whether he has any plans to investigate and identify any accountancy firms which market off-balance sheet financing schemes.
Mr. Redwood: No. I refer the hon. Member to the replies I gave to his questions on 4 and 5 April, Official Report, columns 621 and 802.

section.title: Companies (Fixed Assets)
section.p: Mr. Austin Mitchell: To ask the Secretary of State for Trade and Industry whether he will propose legislation to require all public companies to show market values of their fixed assets.
Mr. Redwood: I have no plans to extend the existing requirements.

section.title: Industrial Cost Accounting
section.p: Mr. Austin Mitchell: To ask the Secretary of State for Trade and Industry whether he has any plans to reduce the influence of historic cost accounting on the financial statements of large limited companies.
Mr. Redwood: No. I refer the hon. Member to the reply I gave to his question on 19 March, Official Report, column 432.

section.title: Company Legislation
section.p: Mr. Austin Mitchell: To ask the Secretary of State for Trade and Industry whether he plans to introduce any legislation to require shareholders to be informed of the company's policy for controlling pollution.

Mr. Redwood: No. It would be burdensome to require companies to provide such information. Companies are best placed to decide, in the light of their individual circumstances, whether such information is likely to be of interest to their members. Interested members may in any case put questions on this subject at the annual general meeting.

Mr. Austin Mitchell: To ask the Secretary of State for Trade and Industry whether he will seek to introduce legislation to require companies (a) to state their environmental policies in their annual report and (b) to inform their shareholders of the number of times they have violated any anti-pollution laws.

Mr. Redwood: No. It would be unreasonably burdensome to require companies to provide such information. Companies are best placed to decide, in the light of their individual circumstances, whether such information is likely to be of interest to their members and other users of their reports and accounts. Interested shareholders may in any case put questions on these subjects at the annual general meeting.

section.title: Steel Industry
section.p: Mrs. Fyfe: To ask the Secretary of State for Trade and Industry if he will make a statement on the future of the steel industry in the United Kingdom.
Mr. Douglas Hogg: I am confident that the United Kingdom steel industry will continue to perform well now that all of it is in the private sector.

section.title: Company Records
section.p: 247. Mr. Campbell-Savours: To ask the Secretary of State for Trade and Industry how many microfiches on average are required to carry the records of a single registered company: and what is the material cost of reproducing a single microfiche for the purpose of supplying the record to an inquirer.
Mr. Redwood: The average number of fiches duplicated per search is 4·5. The average material cost—the cost of the duplicate film only—is 8·5p per search; 1·9 per fiche.

section.title: Regional Policy
section.p: Mr. Win Griffiths: To ask the Secretary of State for Trade and Industry when he next expects to meet his European counterparts to discuss regional policy.
Mr. Douglas Hogg: An informal meeting of EC Regional Policy Ministers has been called at Turin on 23 and 24 November 1990. The United Kingdom will be represented at ministerial level.

section.title: Textile Industry
section.p: Mr. Pike: To ask the Secretary of State for Trade and Industry what recent representations he has received from the textile industry.

Mr. Douglas Hogg: The Department has received a number of representations from the textile industry; my right hon. Friend the Secretary of State has arranged to meet representatives of the industry on 29 October.

section.title: Securities and Investments Board
section.p: Ms. Armstrong: To ask the Secretary of State for Trade and Industry when he next expects to meet the chairman of the Securities and Investments Board to discuss City regulation.

Mr. Redwood: My right hon. Friend and I meet the chairman of the Securities and Investments Board to discuss a range of topics concerning the regulation of financial services as frequently as is necessary. No date has been fixed for the next meeting of this sort.

section.title: Shares
section.p: Dr. Kim Howells: To ask the Secretary of State for Trade and Industry what was the proportion of shares owned by individuals, as opposed to shareholders in general, in 1979 and in 1990.

Mr. Redwood: The stock exchange survey of share ownership carried out in 1981, estimated that in that year 28·2 per cent. of shares were held in the personal sector. Figures for 1979 and 1990 are not available. The value of individuals' holdings has risen substantially over the last decade.

section.title: Animal Skins (Export)
section.p: Mr. Tony Banks: To ask the Secretary of State for Trade and Industry if he will give details of the countries to which United Kingdom-produced animal skins are exported; and what has been the value of that trade in each of the last three years.

Mr. Sainsbury: The only information available is for total United Kingdom exports of raw hides, skins and furskins—SITC division 21. It is published by country in "Overseas Trade Statistics", a copy of which is in the House of Commons Library. These data do not distinguish between United Kingdom-produced goods, and goods previously imported into the United Kingdom.

section.title: European Regional Fund
section.p: Mr. Shore: To ask the Secretary of State for Trade and Industry what payments were made to the United Kingdom from the European regional fund in 1987, 1988 and 1989; and what is the estimate for funds to be received in 1990.

Mr. Douglas Hogg [holding answer 19 October 1990]: United Kingdom payments receipts from the European regional development fund in 1987, 1988 and 1989 were valued at £321 million, £351 million and £386 million, respectively. Payments in 1990 are expected to exceed £400 million.

section.title: Industry Council
section.p: Ms. Quin: To ask the Secretary of State for Trade and Industry which Government Minister attended the European Community Industry Council meeting on 21 September.
Mr. Douglas Hogg [holding answer 22 October 1990]: The Industry Council meeting on 21 September was postponed until 15 October, and I attended that meeting.
Ms. Quin: To ask the Secretary of State for Trade and Industry if he will make a statement on the European Community Industry Council meeting held on 21 September.

Mr. Douglas Hogg [holding answer 22 October 1990]: The Council meeting on 15 October discussed industrial
133 policy, state aids, steel and textiles, and considered Commission communications to the Council on industrial co-operation with eastern Europe and on the Community aerospace industry.

section.title: European Regional Development Fund
section.p: Mr. Win Griffiths: To ask the Secretary of State for Trade and Industry if he will list the annual sums of money committed since the inception of the European regional development fund to each recipient local authority by eligible standard planning region and the annual amount paid to each from the fund.
Mr. Douglas Hogg [holding answer 22 October 1990]: The information requested is not readily available and could be provided only at disproportionate cost.

section.title: EC Stocks
section.p: Mr. John Marshall: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food what is the current level of European Community intervention on stocks of beef.

Mr. Curry: A note setting out the volume of poublic intervention stocks and stocks under aided private storage in the EC and the United Kingdom, which includes figures for beef, is deposited in the Library of the House and is updated on a monthly basis.

section.title: Live Animals (Exports)
section.p: Mr. Cousins: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food if he will list the total numbers of exports of live animals and birds, broken down by species group and point of destination, between (a) the European Community, (b) elsewhere in Europe and (c) further afield, for the last year.
Mr. Curry: The total number of live animals exported from the United Kingdom to the European Community, elsewhere in Europe and further afield during 1989 are listed by species in the table.

td.i: United Kingdom exports of live animals in 1989 by area of destination

section.p: Source: Her Majesty's Customs and Excise.

Mr. Cousins: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food what was the number of inspections of the conditions of live animals and birds being transported live for export in the last year; and what was the number and type of further action which occurred as a result of such inspections.

Mr. Maclean: During 1989, 801,840 animals (farm animals for slaughter, further fattening or breeding and horses and ponies for breeding, riding or recreational purposes) were exported from Great Britain following veterinary inspection for fitness to travel at export lairages near the ports of departure. A total of 8,030 animals were found at inspection to be unfit for the export journey. These were detained, and given veterinary treatment where necessary, until considered fit to travel to an alternative destination in this country.

In addition veterinary inspections are carried out at premises of origin, in accordance with the health requirements of importing countries, for most breeding livestock, horses and ponies, poultry and other mammals and birds. Records are not kept centrally of the number of these inspections.

section.title: Condemned Meat
section.p: Mr. McAvoy: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food if he has received any representations about the sale of condemned meat in butchers' shops and supermarkets; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Maclean: I am aware that there is concern about allegations of illegal trade in unfit meat. I deplore those who seek to pass off such material for human consumption. However, there is already legislation in this area under which action may be taken. The Food Act makes it an offence to sell, hold for sale or prepare for sale for human consumption any material which is unfit for that purpose; the Slaughterhouses Act 1974 requires slaughterhouses and knackers' yards to be licensed by local authorities and there are other detailed controls over the movement and treatment of unfit meat and offal. Nevertheless, we have instituted a full review of the existing controls to see if any improvements are desirable, with particular attention to collection of casualty stock from farms.
Enforcement of the legislation is, of course, a matter for local authorities. However MAFF veterinary officers can and do assist and work closely with local authorities in such cases.

section.title: Fur Farms
section.p: Mr. Tony Banks: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food what information he has regarding the number of fox and mink farms in the United Kingdom; and what provisions exist for inspection of such farms.
Mr. Maclean: Information is not collected on the number of fox farms in the United Kingdom.

Officers of the state veterinary service make visits to fur farms as they do to other livestock farms to undertake welfare inspections. At these visits, the accommodation and management practices are taken into account when assessing the welfare of the animals.

There were 50 licensed mink farms in the United Kingdom on 20 February 1990. Licenses run for no longer than a year and no licence is issued or renewed without an inspection by the appropriate agriculture department.

Mr. Tony Banks: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food if his Ministry's inspectors will conduct a veterinary inspection of the fox fur farm run by Grange Farm Poultry Products in Ovenden Wood, Halifax; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Maclean: This farm has already been visited as part of a welfare monitoring exercise. It is not the Ministry's policy to divulge specific details of such inspections but I understand that there was no evidence of a breach of the welfare legislation at the time of the visit.
Mr. Tony Banks: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food (1) if he will make it his policy to prohibit the breeding of foxes for use by the fur trade; and if he will make a statement;
(2) what regulations exist on the size and type of cage housing foxes and minks on fur farms; and if there are any proposals to enforce minimum standards.

Mr. Maclean: There are no specific regulations on the size and type of cages for fur animals, other than the provisions of the Mink (Keeping) Regulations 1975 which require cages to be constructed in such a manner as to prevent escapes. All fur farmers are, however, bound by the Agriculture (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1968, which makes it an offence to cause unnecessary pain or unnecessary distress to animals on agricultural land.

A recommendation on fur farming has recently been adopted under the Council of Europe convention for the protection of animals kept for farming purposes. This recommendation will come into operation within 12 months and will set minimum welfare standards for fur farms. These include the enrichment of the environment by objects that provide suitable stimuli for the fox to gnaw and to play and a secluded area, such as a nest box and shelf. The recommendation is to be reviewed within five years taking account of further research into the welfare requirements of animals kept for fur.

The Farm Animal Welfare Council has reviewed fur farming and did not recommend that the practice be banned. The Government do not intend to introduce a unilateral ban in this country but will continue to work for welfare improvements on an international basis if further research indicates that these are necessary.

section.title: Methane
section.p: Mr. Flynn: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food if the matter of the control of methane discharge from agricultural activity was discussed at the European Agriculture Council on 15–16 October in Luxembourg.
Mr. Curry: This topic was not on the agenda for this Council and was not discussed.

section.title: British Lamb (Compensation)
section.p: Mr. Moate: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food if he will make a statement on the latest position in his negotiations with the French Government to secure compensation for losses suffered by British interests as a result of actions by French citizens in the lamb war; and if he will describe the detailed compensation proposals and the principles on which the compensation is to be based.

Mr. Curry: The French Government have confirmed that compensation for losses arising as a direct result of French producer action will be forthcoming, as was the case for similar incidents in 1986. The Department stands ready to assist traders in preparing individual claims for submission to the French Government.

section.title: Fishing Vessels (Fuel)
section.p: Mr. David Porter: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food if he will make it his policy to bring forward a temporary scheme to alleviate the price of fuel for fishing vessels while the Gulf crisis continues.

Mr. Curry: No. Other industries and the general public are having to adapt to the higher fuel prices during the Gulf crisis without subsidies. There is no reason to treat the fishing industry differently.

Mr. David Porter: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food what research his Department has done into the possibility of hidden subsidies being given by national Governments of some EEC member states to their fishing industry on fuel costs for fishing vessels; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Curry: The Department has not investigated any oil subsidies to the fishing industry. Member states are required to notify the European Commission of any such aid. The Commission has responsibility to ensure that it is informed of all state aids and that these aids are compatible with the treaty. If evidence can be produced of fuel subsidies by any member Government of the EC to their fishing industry, I shall pursue the matter vigorously.

section.title: Quotas
section.p: Mr. David Porter: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food what is his policy on consultation with interested parties, including fishing organisations, before quota swap agreements with other European Community countries are confirmed; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Curry: We consult the principal industry organisations, the National Federation of Fishermen's Organisations and the Scottish Fishermen's Federation. Also potential quota swaps with other member states are discussed with interested producer organisations and at regular quota management meetings at which representatives from all Fisheries Departments and from the non-sector may be present.

Mr. David Porter: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food (1) if he will make a statement on the overfishing of plaice above quota level by Dutch fishermen for the past two years; and what are the implications of this for English east coast fishermen;

(2) what action he proposes to take at the next Council of Fisheries Ministers meeting, to restore confidence in (a) the Dutch Government enforcing quotas on plaice and (b) the overall regulating and monitoring of each country's plaice quota.

Mr. Curry: Enforcement of Dutch quotas is a matter for the Dutch authorities and the European Commission. Recent events have indicated the seriousness with which this issue is regarded in the Netherlands.

section.title: Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy
section.p: Mr. Simon Hughes: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food what steps he has taken to establish whether the BSE infective agent present in pig and poultry feed is subsequently present in pig and poultry excretions; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Curry [holding answer 19 October 1990]: Research into scrapie has found no evidence that the agent is present
137 in the faeces of infected animals. Studies are planned which will determine the infectivity of the gut both from confirmed cases of BSE and from animals experimentally exposed to the disease.

Nevertheless the Government have already taken steps to ensure that BSE-infected material does not enter the food chain. These include the compulsory slaughter and destruction of all animals suspected of having the disease and a ban on the use in human and animal food of those bovine offals most likely to harbour the BSE agent.

section.title: Further Education Qualifications
section.p: 11. Mr. Wareing: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science if he will make a statement on the progress made in reforming qualifications for those aged 16 to 19 years.
78. Mr. Turner: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science if he will make a statement on progress made in reforming qualifications for those aged 16 to 19 years.

Mr. Eggar: The School Examinations and Assessment Council (SEAC) is currently consulting on principles which would govern A-level and AS syllabuses from 1994. The National Council for Vocational Qualifications is in the lead in the reform of vocational qualifications.

section.title: Grant-maintained Schools
section.p: 12. Mr. Amess: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what is the latest number of schools to have applied for grant-maintained status.

Mr. MacGregor: Seventy-two proposals for grant-maintained status have been published following parental ballots. Of these, 66 have so far reached me for decision: I have approved 53, am minded to approve another one and have rejected 12.
15. Dr. Twinn: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what assessment he has made of the benefits grant-maintained schools gain from opting out.

Mr. MacGregor: Grant-maintained schools have many advantages: they are run by local people who know the schools; they can make their own decisions about how to make the best use of resources, including their share of LEA expenditure on centrally provided services; their governors and heads have greater autonomy than is provided by local management of schools, and they are proving very popular with parents.
28. Mr. David Shaw: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science how many schools became grant-maintained in September.

Mr. Eggar: Fifteen schools became grant-maintained at the beginning of the autumn term. Altogether 44 grant-maintained schools are now operating. Applications for grant-maintained status from another nine schools have already been approved.

168. Mr. David Nicholson: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science how many applications for grant-maintained school status have been received in each local education authority in England.

Mr. Eggar: To date, applications for grant-maintained status have been published by the governing bodies of 72 schools. My right hon. Friend has approved 53 applications; he is minded to approve one application and has rejected 12. He will make decisions on another six applications shortly. Proposals for grant-maintained status are awaited from a further six schools where parents have voted in favour of an application. 82. Mr. Ken Hargreaves: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science in how many schools parents and governors have conducted a ballot on grant-maintained status; and what proportion of these ballots have been in favour.
Mr. Eggar: Parental ballots have been held at 107 schools in England. At 79 schools, 74 per cent., parents have voted in favour of an application for grant-maintained status.

Mr. Pawsey: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what steps he intends to take to increase the number of grant-maintained schools; and what he sees and the principle benefits that will flow to such schools as a result.

Mr. Eggar: From 1 November all maintained primary schools with fewer than 300 pupils will become eligible to
139 seek grant-maintained status. The result will be a tripling of the number of schools currently eligible and an important extension of parental choice. It is for parents and governors to decise whether to seek grant-maintained status for their schools. I am sure that in coming to a decision they will want to talk to existing grant-maintained schools. The first grant-maintained schools have been operating for over a year. Pupils have benefited from the greater flexibility which is available to governors and staff. The schools are spending more money on books, equipment and teachers and are developing exciting new ways of making the best use of resources.

section.title: Bradford CTC
section.p: 13. Mr. Cryer: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what is the total amount of grant aid provided in the current year to the most recent practicable date for the city technology college in Bradford.
Mr. Eggar: The total grant paid to Bradford city technology college from 1 January 1990 to 30 September 1990 is £4·513 million. This figure covers capital, transitional and recurrent grant.

section.title: Education Budget
section.p: 14. Mr. Hind: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what proportion of the primary and secondary education budget local authorities are retaining for central administration; and if he will make a statement.

52. Mr. Evennett: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science whether he will consider taking action against local authorities that hold back funds from schools in order to finance central bureaucracy.

Mr. MacGregor: The published budget statements for 1990–91 indicate that the amount which local education authorities are planning to retain for central administration varies from 2 per cent. to 8 per cent. of the funds available for spending by primary and secondary schools. The average is 3·8 per cent.

I am arranging for the details of each local authority's spending on central administration and on other items to be printed in the Official Report. I believe it is essential that as much as possible of the schools budget of local authorities should be given directly to the schools to manage themselves; and I shall be making further proposals to that end later this year.

tr.td: 1990–91 Budgets: Total LMS spending and percentages of potential schools budget
Potential Schools Budget. The amount potentially available for allocation through the LMS formula. Equal to the General Schools Budget (Column 1) less mandatory exceptions (Columns 2 and 3).
Aggregated Schools Budget. The amount planned to be allocated through the LMS formula. Equal to the Potential Schools Budget (Column 4) less discretionary exceptions (Column 5).

Limited excepted items as percentage of General Schools Budget. This measures planned spending on limited discretionary exceptions against the limit of 10 per cent. of the General Schools Budget placed on the total of these items.

Transitional exceptions. Planned spending on activities subject to compulsory competitive tendering (mainly building cleaning and grounds maintenance). This spending will be allocated through the formula following the expiry of initial contracts.

Other unlimited exceptions. Planned spending on advisers and inspectors, dismissals and premature retirements, and governors' insurance. Each item averages under 1 per cent. of the Potential Schools Budget.
Total unlimited exceptions. The total of Columns 9 to 13.

Other limited exceptions. Planned spending on all limited items other than structural repairs and maintenance (Column 15). Mainly insurances, pupils with statements of special educational need, special units, educational psychologists, education welfare officers, peripatetic teachers, pupil support, LEA initiatives, supply teaching, teachers' safeguarding allowances and contingency funds. Each item averages under 1 per cent. of the Potential Schools Budget.
Total limited exceptions. The total of Columns 15 and 16.
Total discretionary exceptions. The total of Columns 14 and 17.
NB.—Where percentages are totalled, slight differences may occur due to rounding.
Calderdale, Hampshire and Waltham Forest have not yet published their budget statements.

Comparisons between authorities will indicate variations due to policy decisions (for example, whether to delegate or retain funds centrally) and the diversity of LEAs' areas (for example, a rural county is likely to have higher home to school transport costs than a London borough). But there will also be differences which are due purely to LMS treatment or accounting practices adopted. The following are the areas most significantly affected:

1. The scope of the General Schools Budget. There is no detailed legal definition of what items are to be included in the GSB. Circular 7/88 indicates the general principle that it should include not only direct institutional costs of schools but also indirect costs for services used by them or attributable to them.

2. Capital spending. The GSB includes spending on capital works. This item is large and will fluctuate widely from year to year and from LEA to LEA. Use of the Potential Schools Budget as the base line, rather than the GSB, largely removes any distortion.

3. Central administration. Although accounting principles recommend that all administration costs should be allocated to front-line services, authorities are free to use a variety of bases for such allocation. Judgment is required—to decide for instance what proportion of costs of central departments such as finance and personnel is attributable to education, and what proportion of the Chief Education Officer's salary relates to LMS schools. There is a large range for spending on central administration—2 per cent. to 8 per cent. of the PSB—but it is unclear how much this range reflects real differences in central bureaucracy and how much merely different accounting judgments.

section.p: 4. Transitional excepted items. There are two possible methods of treating costs of contracts already let for activities subject to competitive tendering. Some LEAs have allocated funds through the formula but schools remain bound by existing contracts; others have retained the costs as an excepted item for the duration of these contracts. Different treatment will not affect schools' freedom but will distort comparisons.

section.title: Teacher Recruitment
section.p: 16. Mr. Fisher: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science if he will make a statement on the progress made in teacher recruitment; and if he will make a statement.
22. Mr. Haselhurst: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science if he will make a statement about the level of teacher recruitment at the start of the new school year.
41. Mr. Hardy: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science if he will make a statement on the progress made in teacher recruitment.
69. Mr. Rooker: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science if he will make a statement on the progress made in teacher recruitment.

Mr. Fallon: The Department's September survey of teacher vacancies showed that LEAs and schools were very successful in filling teaching posts this summer. Teachers are broadly available in sufficient numbers to fill posts. Nevertheless, it is clear that there continue to be difficulties in certain parts of the country and in certain subjects. We shall continue with our range of measures to improve teacher supply.

20. Mr. Simon Hughes: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what are his estimates of the number of unfilled teaching posts in (a) primary and (b) secondary schools in London at the beginning of the autumn term of the current year.

Mr. Fallon: My right hon. Friend published on 5 October the results of the Department's survey of teacher vacancies at the beginning of September. A copy is in the Library. On 3 September LEAs in Greater London reported 311 unfilled posts in primary schools, and 245 unfilled posts in secondary schools. This is very much fewer than the vacancy levels reported in January. These results reflect the good work and determination of authorities to fill their vacancies and show that our measures to improve teacher recruitment and retention are working.

section.title: Church Schools
section.p: 17. Mr. Corbett: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what is his policy towards the provision of free transport to and from voluntary aided church schools by local education authorities.

Mr. Fallon: The Government's view on the provision of school transport for pupils attending denominational schools was given in a circular letter on school transport and choice of school that was sent to all local education authorities in December 1981. That advice remains current. A copy of the letter is in the Library of the House.

section.title: Scottish Education
section.p: 18. Mr. Wallace: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science when he next expects to meet the University Funding Council to discuss the funding of Scottish education.

Mr. Alan Howarth: My right hon. Friend and I meet the chairman and members of the UFC from time to time. Our discussions range over various matters bearing on the council's funding of universities throughout Great Britain. Other aspects of Scottish education are for my right hon. and learned Friend the Secretary of State for Scotland.

section.title: School Premises Regulations 1981
section.p: 19. Mr. Livsey: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science whether he intends to review the School Premises Regulations 1981.
Mr. Fallon: My right hon. Friend announced on 2 October that the DES and the Welsh Office are to conduct a review of the School Premises Regulations.

section.title: Schools (Maintenance)
section.p: 21. Mr. Mullin: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what is the current backlog in repairs and maintenance of schools; and if he will make a statement.
73. Mr. Nellist: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what is the current backlog in repairs and maintenance of schools; and if he will make a statement.
Mr. Fallon: The Department keeps no detailed data on the state of school buildings, which are the responsibility of local education authorities and governors of voluntary aided schools.

A realistic estimate of the cost of remedying deficiencies, based on a survey of school buildings in 1986, is about £2 billion at 1990 prices. Some £2·6 billion at 1990 prices is estimated to have been spent on school building between 1986–87 and 1989–90, mostly on new school places and reorganisation schemes to remove surplus capacity. A substantial proportion will, however, have gone towards remedying deficiencies.
66. Mr. Nicholas Brown: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what proposals he has to improve the physical condition of schools.

Mr. Fallon: The physical condition of maintained schools is the responsibility of local education authorities, shared in the case of voluntary aided schools with governing bodies. It is for them to decide their spending priorities. We are making significant resources available. Annual capital guidelines for capital expenditure on schools and colleges in England are £485 million this year compared with £352 million under the old system of allocations for 1989–90. Local authorities are free to spend above that level by using capital receipts and other sources of income including revenue. In addition, £109 million of grant is available for voluntary schools compared with £86 million available last year.
71. Mr. Crowther: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what representations he has received about the backlog in repairs and maintenance in schools.

Mr. Fallon: My right hon. Friend has received a number of letters and other representations from local education authorities, hon. Members and others about the repair and maintenance of school buildings.
72. Mr. Madden: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science if he will arrange to visit maintained schools in Bradford in need of renovation and repair.
Mr. Fallon: My right hon. Friend plans to visit Bradford on 31 October when he will be shown round Thornbury County first school before going on to open the new city technology college.

section.title: Education, Inner London
section.p: 23. Mr. David Evans: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what assessment has been made so far by his Department of changes in the provision of education in inner London following the abolition of the Inner London education authority.

Mr. Eggar: The new inner London LEAs are making progress towards developing a more effective education service in inner London. They have recruited teachers to fill classroom vacancies, and many are consulting on the reorganisation of school provision.

section.title: Local Management of Schools
section.p: 24. Mr. Riddick: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science if he will make a further statement on the operation of local management of schools; and whether he has any plans to change the operation of local management of schools for the future.

Mr. Fallon: Eighty-seven local education authorities introduced schemes of local management of schools in April. Most head teachers and governors welcome the prospect of greater autonomy in the running of their schools. We are monitoring and reviewing all aspects of local management of schools and will consult later this

td.i: 1990–91 Budgets: Discretionary exceptions and school budgets
LEA ranked by discretionary exceptions per cent, of PSB
Amount available at schools if LEA at average discretionary exceptions per cent. £

section.p: year on proposals, including proposals to increase the proportion of resources available for schools to manage themselves.
30. Ms. Walley: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what representations he has received regarding local management of schools; and if he will make a statement.
48. Dr. Michael Clark: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what representations he has received regarding school budgets under the local management of schools proposals.
Mr. Fallon: I refer my hon. Friend to the reply that I gave to the hon. Member for Newport, West (Mr. Flynn) on 15 October 1990, Official Report, column 642.

43. Mr. Beith: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what assessment he had made of the impact of the financial controls associated with local management of schools on small first schools and primary schools.
Mr. Fallon: I refer the hon. Member to the reply that I gave earlier today to the hon. Member for Burnley (Mr. Pike).

Mr. Pawsey: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science if he will publish a list giving the amount of holdback each local education authority is making in the context of local management of schools, with an indication showing the political control of each such authority; if he will give details of the action he is taking to reduce the amount of holdback; and if he will further set out in the list the amount that would be available for schools if the authority was at the average level of holdback.

Mr. Fallon: The following table provides the relevant information. My right hon. Friend is considering the scope for increased delegation of resources to schools and expects to consult later this year.

section.title: Teachers' Pay
section.p: 25. Mr. Colvin: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science when he expects his proposals for new long-term negotiating machinery on teachers' pay to be operative.
Mr. Eggar: My right hon. Friend has made it clear that he intends to introduce legislation at the earliest opportunity to establish new permanent pay negotiating machinery for teachers.

38. Mr. Holt: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what were the average earnings for teachers in (a) primary, (b) secondary and (c) higher and further education in each major EEC country for the latest year for which statistics are available; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Eggar: Some information on EC teachers' salaries in 1985 is published in a detailed research report "The Conditions of Service of Teachers in the European Community", published by the European Commission in 1988 (pages 133 to 160). A copy is available in the Library.
60. Mr. Yeo: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what recent representations he has received regarding teachers' pay.
Mr. Eggar: My right hon. Friend receives frequent representations from the teacher unions and others about teachers' pay and conditions.

84. Mr. Dykes: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science if he will make a statement on the response from interested parties to his proposals for local authority discretion in teachers' pay bargaining, announced on 23 July.
Mr. Barry Field: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what representations he has received in response to his proposals for a new pay negotiating machinery for teachers.

Mr. Eggar: My right hon. Friend has received a number of representations from the teacher unions and others commenting on aspects of his proposals to establish new pay determination machinery for teachers.

section.title: Special Needs Education
section.p: 26. Mr. Boyes: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what representations he has received regarding local management of schools and children with special educational needs; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Fallon: My right hon. Friend has received a number of representations concerning provision for pupils with special educational needs in schools covered by schemes of local management. In response we have confirmed our concern that appropriate and effective provision should be made for pupils with special educational needs. The introduction of LMS does not alter authorities' responsibilities for pupils with special educational needs and should have no adverse effect on provision for such pupils.

Mr. Battle: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science whether formula funding arrangements under 156 local management of schools will take account of resources needed in schools to prevent statementing; when calculating special needs provision.
Mr. Fallon: Local management of schools offers local education authorities the flexibility to take account of the resources needed in schools to support all pupils with special educational needs.

section.title: City Technology Colleges
section.p: 27. Mr. Grocott: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what recent developments there have been in the city technology college programme; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Fallon: The CTC programme is making substantial progress. Four colleges opened last month bringing the total of operational colleges to seven. Seven more are planned to open in 1991. My right hon. Friend has this month initiated consultation on proposals from the Wolfson Foundation and Cable and Wireless plc for a further college to serve the city of Bristol. If established the Bristol CTC will open in 1992.
55. Mrs. Maureen Hicks: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what interest has been expressed by parents in the establishment of city technology colleges.

Mr. Fallon: Parents are expressing their confidence in the city technology college programme by seeking places for their children in overwhelming numbers. All the colleges which are open have been oversubscribed in applications for places, both in initial and in subsequent years.

section.title: Student Accommodation
section.p: 29. Dr. Moonie: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science if he will make a statement on student accommodation.
37. Mr. Doran: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science if he will make a statement on student accommodation.
Mr. Alan Howarth: I refer the hon. Members to the reply that I gave earlier today to the hon. Member for Edinburgh, South (Mr. Griffiths).

section.title: School-Business Links
section.p: 31. Mr. Ian Bruce: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science how many schools have links with local businesses.

Mr. Fallon: A recent survey by the Department indicated that around 90 per cent. of secondary schools and 54 per cent. of primary schools have links with local businesses. The findings of the survey were published in August as a DES Statistical Bulletin, a copy of which is in the Library.
80. Mr. Robert B. Jones: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what initiatives he is pursuing to ensure schools have closer links with industry.

Mr. Fallon: The Department is working with other Government Departments, links bodies and employers in
157 a range of initiatives designed to further the growth of links between schools and industry. In particular, we are taking forward an initiative to support local education business partnerships which will have a broad balance of membership from local business, education and community interests. The Department also selectively funds individual projects and organisations, publishes and distributes information and guides to good practice, and encourages the incorporation of economic and industrial dimensions into the school curriculum.

section.title: Language Learning
section.p: 32. Sir Hal Miller: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what steps he is taking to ensure that young people have an effective grounding in a modern foreign language.
68. Mr. Hague: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what importance he places on langague learning.

Mr. Eggar: The Government are concerned to increase both the number of pupils continuing to study a modern foreign language until age 16 and beyond, and their standards of language competence. That is why the national curriculum includes a modern foreign language as a foundation subject to be studied by all pupils aged 11 to 16 in maintained secondary schools. My right hon. Friends the Secretaries of State for Education and Science and for Wales will be publishing shortly their proposals for attainment targets and programmes of study for modern foreign languages in the national curriculum, together with the final report of the working group for modern foreign languages, on whose recommendations my right hon. Friends' proposals are based. We aim to start implementing the attainment targets and programmes of study in schools from autumn 1992.

section.title: Student Loans
section.p: 33. Mr. McFall: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science if he will make a statement on the operation of the student loans scheme and access funds.
53. Mr. Watson: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science if he will make a statement on the operation of the student loans scheme and access funds.
64. Mr. Robert Hughes: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science if he will make a statement on the operation of the student loans scheme and access funds.
Mr. Alan Howarth: I refer the hon. Members to the reply that I gave earlier today to the hon. Member for Edinburgh, Central (Mr. Darling).
47. Mr. Canavan: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science how many representations he has received in the current year about student loans.
Mr. Alan Howarth: We have received a substantial number of representations about the introduction of student loans and related aspects of the Government's student support policy.

section.title: Hackney (Financial Aid)
section.p: 34. Mr. Sedgemore: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what further financial assistance he intends to give the London borough of Hackney.

Mr. Eggar: We shall give careful consideration to Hackney local education authority's bids for funding for capital expenditure and for activities within the combined grants for education support and training programme for 1991–92, alongside those received from other LEAs.

section.title: Research Councils
section.p: 35. Dr. Thomas: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what is the total amount of money currently allocated to each of the research councils; and what was the comparable figure in (a) 1979 and (b) 1985.

Mr. Alan Howarth: The figures are as follows:
£ million (cash)
1979–80 1985–86 1990–91
AFRC 29·5 52·7 86·2
ESRC 16·8 23·6 36·2
MRC 68·0 122·3 185·7
NERC 36·6 67·9 136·0
SERC 175·6 298·4 437·4
In real terms the total allocation to the research councils increased by 26·5 per cent. over the period.

section.title: Under-fives
section.p: 36. Mr. Wray: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science if he will make a statement on public funding of playgroups and nurseries for under-fives.

Mr. Eggar: Playgroups and other forms of sessional and day care are the responsibility at national level of my right hon. and learned Friend the Secretary of State for Health. However, my Department makes an annual grant, currently £179,000, to the Pre-school Playgroups Association for activities contributing to the educational improvement of playgroups. In 1991–92 the Department will support under the grants for education support and training arrangements a total of £2·5 million of expenditure by local education authorities on improving the planning and co-ordination of provision for the under-fives; this includes work in educational settings and the educational component of playgroups.
39. Mr. Jim Marshall: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what proposals he has to increase the number of nursery education places for three and four-year-olds.
45. Mr. Fearn: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science whether he will make a statement on local authority provision for the under-fives.
65. Mr. Henderson: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what proposals he has to increase the number of nursery education places for three and four-year-olds.
81. Mrs. Dunwoody: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what proposals he has to increase the number of nursery education places for three and four-year-olds.

Mr. Eggar: The Government believe in a diversity of provision for the under-fives, and considers that local authorities are best placed to determine the extent and range of provision in their area. Over the last decade, the
159 numbers of under-fives attending nursery or primary classes in England have increased by nearly 35 per cent. Provisional data for 1990 show that in the last year the numbers rose from 548,000 to 577,000 and the age participation rate from 45 per cent. to 47 per cent.

section.title: Parental Choice
section.p: 40. Mr. Hanley: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science whether he has considered the implications for his policy on parental choice of the Greenwich judgment; and if he will make a statement.
Mr. Fallon: My right hon. Friend is aware of the Greenwich judgment, and will be looking closely at its effect on the pattern of school admissions.

section.title: Science Budget
section.p: 42. Mr. Cousins: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science when he last met the Advisory Board for the Research Councils to discuss the science budget for 1990–91 and 1991–92.
Mr. Alan Howarth: My right hon. Friend met and discussed the science budget with the board on 24 July 1990.

section.title: Primary Schools, Staffordshire
section.p: 44. Mr. Knox: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science how much was spent per pupil at primary schools in Staffordshire in the most recent year for which figures are available; and what was the comparable figure in 1978–79 at constant prices.
Mr. Fallon: Staffordshire spent some £1,050 per nursery and primary pupil in 1988–89. At 1988–89 prices the figure for 1978–79 was some £820. This represents an increase of some 28 per cent.

section.title: Surplus School Places
section.p: 46. Ms. Quin: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what is the current number of surplus places in schools.
58. Mr. Clelland: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science if he will make a statement on the number of surplus places in schools.

Mr. Fallon: The latest estimate is that in January 1989 there were approximately 830,000 surplus primary school places and 950,000 surplus secondary school places in England. Local education authorities have removed about 100,000 surplus places over each of the past five years, although this reduction has been offset to some extent by the need to provide additional places in areas of population growth. We have repeatedly enjoined LEAs to do more to save money by rationalising their school provision.

section.title: Erasmus Project
section.p: 49. Mrs. Margaret Ewing: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science how many students in the academic year 1990–91 have applied and how many have been accepted to take part in the Erasmus project.

56. Mr. Sillars: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science how many students in the academic year 1990–91 have applied, and how many have been accepted, to take part in the Erasmus project.
Mr. Alan Howarth: I refer the hon. Members to the reply that I gave to the hon. Member for Angus, East (Mr. Welsh) on 15 October 1990, Official Report, col. 640.

section.title: Rural Schools
section.p: 50. Mr. Alex Carlile: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what plans he has to help small rural schools implement the national curriculum.

Mr. Eggar: The Government are giving local education authorities specific grant support for the introduction of the national curriculum. Grants will support some £120 million LEA expenditure in England this financial year, rising to nearly £170 million expenditure next financial year. This is in addition to general revenue support grant funding for local authority spending. It is for individual authorities to decide, in the light of local needs and priorities, how much to spend to help small rural schools to deliver the national curriculum.

section.title: Teacher Supply
section.p: 51. Mr. Geraint Howells: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science whether he will make a statement on teacher supply.
61. Mr. Steinberg: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science if he will make a statement on the current level of teacher supply.
62. Ms. Harman: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science whether he will make a statement on the current level of teacher supply.

Mr. Fallon: My right hon. Friend published on 5 October the results of the Department's survey of teacher vacancies at the beginning of September. A copy is in the Library. The results show that LEAs and schools were very successful in filling teaching posts this summer and that teachers are broadly available in sufficient numbers to fill posts. Nevertheless, it is clear that there continue to be difficulties in certain parts of the country and in certain subjects. We shall continue with our range of measures to improve teacher recruitment and retention.

section.title: School Books
section.p: 54. Mr. McWilliam: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what representations he has received about the supply of books in schools.

Mr. Fallon: My right hon. Friend has received representations from educational publishers and from some schools and LEAs about the supply of books, including school books, to support the introduction of the national curriculum. In response to these representations, my right hon. Friend has announced a new activity within the grants for education support and training programme for 1991–92 which will support £15 million expenditure on books for the national curriculum. The representations are also being taken into account in considering the 1991–92 local authority grant settlement.

section.title: Haringey (Education Quality)
section.p: 57. Mr. Butler: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what information he has on the quality of education in Haringey; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Fallon: Her Majesty's inspectorate routinely provides reports on education provision in Haringey as part of its normal inspection programme. The London borough of Haringey also provides information to the Department as requested from time to time on a number of aspects of educational provision.

section.title: Seven-year-olds (Testing)
section.p: 59. Mr. Haynes: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science if he will make a statement on his deliberations about standardised testing for seven-year-olds.
79. Mr. Rogers: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science if he will make a statement on his deliberations about standardised testing for seven-year-olds.
75. Mr. Barron: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what representations he has received regarding standard assessment tests for seven-year-olds; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Eggar: I refer the hon. Members to the reply that my right hon. Friend the Secretary of State gave earlier today to the hon. Member for Redcar (Ms. Mowlam) and my hon. Friend the Member for Harrow, West (Mr. Hughes).

section.title: AIDS
section.p: 63. Mr. Strang: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science when he last met the chairman of the Medical Research Council to discuss research into AIDS.
Mr. Alan Howarth: My right hon. Friend is kept fully informed about the progress of the council's programme of research into AIDS, and received a presentation on this in March.

section.title: Teacher Training
section.p: 67. Mr. Nicholas Bennett: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science whether he has any plans to reform teacher training.

Mr. Fallon: The Government's aim is constantly to improve the quality of teacher training. Recent innovations have included the introduction of revised criteria for the approval of initial teacher training courses; shortened BEd courses; extended PGCE courses in shortage subjects; the licensed teacher scheme for mature entrants to teaching; and school-based articled teacher schemes, starting this autumn. The effectiveness of these arrangements is being kept under review and further improvements will be introduced as necessary.

section.title: National Curriculum
section.p: Mr. Win Griffiths: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science if he will make a statement on progress on the implementation of the national curriculum.
70. Mr. Buckley: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science if he will make a statement on the implementation of the national curriculum.

Mr. Eggar: There is welcome evidence from Her Majesty's inspectorate that most schools are making satisfactory or good progress in implementing the national curriculum. My right hon. Friend is taking steps to ensure that the new requirements are phased in gradually over a number of years, subject by subject, to make implementation more manageable for teachers.

section.title: Mature Students
section.p: 74. Mrs. Heal: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what impact the access funds have had on mature students.
Mr. Alan Howarth: It is too early to say. The access funds scheme has only just started.

section.title: Classrooms (Toxic Substances)
section.p: 76. Mr. Sumberg: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science if he will take steps to ban the use of typewriter correcting fluid and other similar toxic substances in school classrooms.

Mr. Fallon: Many substances which have useful applications in schools may be toxic if they are misused. For this reason the national curriculum requires that all young people should be educated about the dangers of solvent and other substance misuse in science and technology; and the Department of Education and Science has issued guidance to LEAs and schools on the safe handling of volatile substances. My right hon. Friend has no powers to take further steps.

section.title: Disabled People
section.p: 77. Mr. Wigley: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science whether he has any plans to launch a full survey on disabled access to (a) colleges of further education, (b) colleges of higher education and (c) universities in the United Kingdom.
Mr. Alan Howarth: My right hon. Friend has no such plans.

section.title: Education, Outer London
section.p: 83. Mr. Jessel: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what information he has on trends in educational standards in outer London boroughs.

Mr. Eggar: The following table indicates trends in public examination results for school leavers in the outer London boroughs since 1982. The national curriculum assessment system, when fully in place at all key stages, will, when combined with improved methods of collecting and reporting data on examination results, provide a fuller and more accurate picture.

td.i: Outer London local education authorities maintained schools Percentage of school leavers at a range of levels of achievement

section.p: A large proportion of 1+ A-level achievers are also counted in 5+ grades A-C/1.

Richmond-upon-Thames provides all A-level teaching through a tertiary system. Other local education authorities have adopted alternative modes of tertiary provision and this may well have a bearing on A-level figures.

The above data is based on a 10 per cent. survey. Since figures from small local education authorities are subject to relatively large levels of sampling error, figures are taken over a three year period.
Source: Statistics of Education—School Leavers (DES) 1984–88.

section.title: Education Reform
section.p: 85. Mr. Colin Shepherd: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what plans he has to meet local authority associations to discuss progress of the Education Reform Act.
Mr. Eggar: My right hon. Friend meets the local authority associations from time to time to discuss various aspects of the Government's educational reforms and other issues.

section.title: GCSE
section.p: Mr. Rowlands: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what average grade has been achieved by pupils sitting GCSE in recent years in each of the core and foundation subjects established by the Education Act.

Mr. Fallon: The table shows, for 15-year-old pupils in England in 1988–89, the percentage of those attempting each national curriculum subject who gain a grade A-C or D-G. The only year for which information is available in this form is 1988–89.

section.title: Truancy
section.p: Mr. Pawsey: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what action he is taking to reduce truancy.

Mr. Fallon: My right hon. Friend is providing funds, through education support grant, for projects designed to improve attenance in designated schools in a total of 31 local education authorities. Last year the Department published a survey report by Her Majesty's inspectorate which reviews school attendance and calls attention to examples of good practice in schools and local education authorities.
My right hon. Friend is considering the need for additional measures to secure improvements in the vital area of school attendance.

section.title: Schools (Fire Damage)
section.p: Mr. Pawsey: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what information he has on the number of schools, and of what type, which have been extensively damaged by fire during the last 12 months and on the comparable figure for 1980.
Mr. Fallon: The Department does not maintain records of the number of schools damaged by fire.

Mr. Pawsey: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what guidance is given to local education authorities in respect of the desirability of insurance against fire of school premises and the type of security provided against fire and arson in school premises; and what plans he has to review the guidance.

Mr. Fallon: The Department does not issue guidance to local education authorities on the desirability of insurance against fire of school premises. Guidance on precautions against fire, including arson attacks, is published in the Department's building bulletins. This guidance is under constant review.

section.title: School Discipline
section.p: Mr. Pawsey: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what evidence he has received indicating trends in the level of school discipline.

Mr. Fallon: My right hon. Friend has received no recent evidence about trends in the level of school discipline. The report of the committee of inquiry into discipline in schools, chaired by my noble Friend Lord Elton, did however include the findings of a large-scale survey of school discipline. That survey, conducted in nearly 500 schools in autumn 1988, identified persistent low-level disruption as the most common disciplinary problem.

section.title: Education Spending
section.p: Mr. Pawsey: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what was education spending per pupil in 1990–91, 1984–85 and 1979–80; and if he will set out the figures by reference to primary schools and secondary schools.

Mr. Fallon: The latest available figures on outturn recurrent spending in schools relate to 1988–89. The table shows school-based spending per pupil in that year, compared with spending in 1979–80 and 1984–85. The spending returns group nursery schools with primary schools.
The figures are in cash terms. They do not include spending on central LEA services such as transport and administration, or any capital spending.

section.title: Class Sizes
section.p: Mr. Pawsey: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what was the average size of secondary and primary school classes in 1979–80, 1984–85 and 1990–91.

Mr. Fallon: Information for 1990–91 is not yet available. The average class sizes in 1979–80, 1984–85 and 1989–90 in maintained primary and secondary schools in England were as follows:
11979–80 11984–85 11989–90 provisional
Primary2 25·4 24·9 25·9
Secondary2 20·9 20·4 20·0
