My Department has also been advised, in confidence, of several other proposals for new gas turbine generating stations. It will be for the companies concerned to decide when to make public details of these proposals.

section.title: AGR Refuelling
section.p: Mr. Dobson: To ask the Secretary of State for Energy what percentage of refuelling is currently being achieved on load by each Nuclear Electric advanced gas-cooled reactor.
Mr. Wakeham: This is an operational matter for Nuclear Electric.

section.title: Electricity Distribution Companies
section.p: Mr. Dobson: To ask the Secretary of State for Energy what valuation his advisers have placed on each of the electricity distribution companies, including their share of the National Grid Company.

Mr. Wakeham: The value of the regional electricity companies will depend on a wide range of factors including each company's share of National Grid Holdings plc and on market conditions at the time of sale. Details of the capital structures, future prospects as well as profit and dividend forecasts for each company will be included in the prospectus.
Mr. Dobson: To ask the Secretary of State for Energy what are the estimated profits and dividends, respectively, of each of the electricity distribution companies.
Mr. Wakeham: Details of the capital structures, future prospects as well as profit and dividend forecasts for each company will be included in the prospectus.

section.title: National Power and PowerGen
section.p: Mr. Dobson: To ask the Secretary of State for Energy on what date he agreed the debt to be borne by National Power and PowerGen.
Mr. Wakeham: Agreement on the amount of debt to be issued by PowerGen and National Power on flotation was reached in August and September 1990 respectively.

section.title: Vibration White Finger
section.p: Mr. Cummings: To ask the Secretary of State for Energy what is the anticipated number of ex-employees and employees of British Coal, by region, who are suffering from vibration white finger; and if he will make a statement.
Mr. Baldry: This is a matter for the British Coal Corporation.

section.title: Correspondence
section.p: Mr. Steinberg: To ask the Secretary of State for Energy what is the average time his Department takes in replying to an hon. Member's letter; and what is (a) the shortest time and (b) the longest time it has taken to reply in full to an hon. Member's letter in the last Session of Parliament.

Mr. Wakeham: The Department's general objective is to answer letters from hon. Members within three weeks of receipt. The specific information requested by the hon. Member could be obtained only at disproportionate cost.

section.title: Privatisation Vetting Committee
section.p: Mr. Dobson: To ask the Secretary of State for Energy for what reasons the privatisation vetting committee told the chairman of Eastern Electricity that he should not address the Energy Industries Club on Thursday 25 October.
Mr. Wakeham: The decision not to address the Energy Industries Club was taken by the chairman, Dr. James Smith and no advice was sought or issued from a committee.

section.title: North Sea Gas
section.p: Mr. Steinberg: To ask the Secretary of State for Energy if he will list the latest calculations of gas reserves in the North sea.

Mr. Moynihan: The latest estimate of remaining gas reserves on the United Kingdom continental shelf is given in the latest edition of the publication "Development of the Oil and Gas Resources of the United Kingdom" [the Brown Book] which my right hon. Friend presented to Parliament on 30 April 1990.

section.title: Plutonium
section.p: Mr. Flynn: To ask the Secretary of State for Energy if he will set out, in regard to departmental news release number 195 concerning annual civil plutonium figures, the specific quantities of plutonium exported to Austria, Belgium, the Federal Republic of Germany and France, respectively, as mentioned in footnote 4(a); if he will list the safeguard agreements covering this exported plutonium; and what amounts of plutonium were involved per annum sent temporarily to France as mentioned in footnote 4(b,ii).

Mr. Baldry: Quantities of exports of civil plutonium to individual countries cannot be disclosed on the grounds of commercial confidentiality. Each country listed has a safeguards agreement with the International Atomic Energy Agency; the texts are in IAEA INFCIRCs 156 (Austria/IAEA), 193 (Euratom/Non Nuclear Weapon States/IAEA) and 290 (France/Euratom/IAEA) respectively.

section.title: Combined Heat and Power
section.p: Mr. Cummings: To ask the Secretary of State for Energy if he will make a statement concerning Her Majesty's Government's interest in promoting combined heat and power plants.
Mr. Baldry: I will write to the hon. Member as soon as possible.

section.title: Oil Companies (Gifts)
section.p: Mr. Austin Mitchell: To ask the Secretary of State for Energy, further to his answer of 15 October, Official Report, column 681, concerning entertainment or gifts offered by oil companies, (1) whether he will publish the names of the oil companies that made the five gifts, the ranks and duties of the officials to whom the gifts were made, the nature of the gift and the reason for accepting it and whether the gifts were handed over to establishment division for disposal;

(2) whether he will publish in the Official Report a table, showing for each of the oil companies the number of invitations made and the number accepted in 1989, together with a breakdown into such categories of entertainment as are distinguished in the records maintained.
Mr. Moynihan: As the answer given on 15 October at column 681 made clear, there are specific rules laid down for the acceptance of gifts and entertainment by civil servants.
I am satisfied that these procedures have been followed.

section.title: House Building
section.p: Mr. Murphy: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales how many new houses were started by Welsh local authorities in the most recent year for which figures are available.
Mr. Grist: In 1989, a total of 501 new dealings were started by local authorities.
Mr. Murphy: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales what resources he intends to allocate to Welsh district councils for new house building.

Mr. Grist: It is too early to say what resources will be available next year. However, it is a matter for each local authority to determine its own housing priorities within the resources available to it taking account of local needs and securing value for money.

section.title: Tai Cymru
section.p: Mr. Murphy: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales if he intends to appoint to the board of Tai Cymru any representatives of Welsh local authorities.
Mr. Grist: My right hon. Friend has no plans at this stage to appoint any new members to the board of Tai Cymru.

Mr. David Hunt: I shall write to the hon. Gentleman and place a copy of my letter in the Library of the House.

section.title: Housing (Waiting Lists)
section.p: Mr. Murphy: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales how many people are on local authority housing waiting lists in Wales.
Mr. Grist: The information is not collected centrally.

section.title: Denominational Education
section.p: Mr. Murphy: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales if he intends to continue supporting denominational education in Wales.
Sir Wyn Roberts: I will continue my support for denominational education in Wales as part of the Government's overall policy for choice in education.

section.title: Welsh Language
section.p: Mr. Murphy: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales what extra resources he intends to make available for the compulsory teaching of Welsh, particularly in non-native Welsh-speaking areas such as Gwent.

Sir Wyn Roberts: Grants for in-service training of teachers in Welsh was increased from £223,000 in the financial year 1989–90 to £ 1 million in 1990–91. This will be further increased to £1·64 million in 1991–92. Additionally, £0·5 million is available through the grants for education support and training scheme for the appointment of specialist training advisers in each LEA and the Welsh Joint Education Committee. Areas such as Gwent will also benefit from other initiatives, supported by Welsh Office funding, to develop teaching materials for pupils studying Welsh as a second language and the award of financial incentives to student teachers.

Mr. Murphy: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales what effect he expects the requirement of the national curriculum in Wales for the compulsory teaching of Welsh to GCSE level to have on the teaching of modern languages.

Sir Wyn Roberts: The national curriculum in Wales includes both Welsh and a modern foreign language. This will increase the number of pupils who study a modern foreign language. It is not intended that pupils should be required to study Welsh to GCSE level: there is the alternative for 14 to 16-year-olds of a more limited programme of study taking up about half the time of a GCSE course.

The Welsh Office has been consulting education interests in Wales about the structure of key stage 4 of the national curriculum, including the possibility of greater flexibility and choice. A copy of the consultation letter will be placed in the Library of the House.

section.title: Inside Lavatories
section.p: Mr. Murphy: To ask the Secretary of State for Wales how many houses in Wales are without inside lavatories.
Mr. Grist: In 1986, a total of 20,800 dwellings in Wales lacked a WC inside the dwelling.

section.title: Retirement Pension
section.p: Sir David Price: To ask the Secretary of State for Social Security what percentage of people currently retiring will receive more than the basic rate by way of retirement pension.

Mrs. Gillian Shephard: The precise information requested is not available. However, during the six-month period ending 31 March 1989, 57 per cent, of those awarded basic retirement pension received an additional pension from the state earnings-related pension scheme. Many pensioners also received a small award from the earlier graduated retirement pension scheme. In addition, the latest figures available—for 1987—show that 73 per cent, of all recently retired pensioners receive additional income from occupational pensions.
Mr. Cummings: To ask the Secretary of State for Social Security if he will list the number of state retirement pensioners in Easington in each of the last five years.
Mrs. Gillian Shephard: This information is not available.

section.title: Community Charge Benefit
section.p: Mr. Redmond: To ask the Secretary of State for Social Security what was the community charge benefit case load, as at 30 September, for the Doncaster standard region.

Mrs. Gillian Shephard: The 31 August 1990 quarterly count of community charge benefit claims in local authorities is not yet available. However, the number of community charge benefit claims as at 31 May 1990 for the Doncaster standard region was 660,000—couples count as
667 one. The May 1990 data reflect a time when local authorities in England and Wales were coping with the introduction of the community charge scheme and were faced with large numbers of unprocessed claims. The May 1990 figure of 660,000 is, therefore, likely to understate the true position.

section.title: Kuwait Invasion
section.p: Mr. Alfred Morris: To ask the Secretary of State for Social Security if any increase is planned in the resources available to the social fund to allow for the unpredictable extra expenditure incurred in helping people who have returned to the United Kingdom from Iraq and Kuwait since the invasion of Kuwait.
Mr. Scott: All such expenditure is being recorded and monitored. At this stage it is not thought that extra resources will be required, but close monitoring will continue.

section.title: Income Support
section.p: Mr. Maxton: To ask the Secretary of State for Social Security how many requests for attachment to income support in connection with non-payment of the community charge have been made by each regional and island council in Scotland; and how many requests for attachments for outstanding community charge debts have been refused because there were too many existing attachments.

Mrs. Gillian Shephard: No records are maintained in local offices of the number of applications made by individual local authorities for deductions from income support to clear community charge arrears. No information is available on the reason for refusal of requests for deductions from income support.

Mr. Tony Banks: To ask the Secretary of State for Social Security how many income support claimants are still receiving transitional protection and have not had a benefit increase since 1987; how many of these are people with disabilities; and how many are pensioners.

Mrs. Gillian Shephard: Shortly after last April's uprating benefits, the number of income support claimants receiving statutory transitional additions was about 110,000. About 86,000 of these were receiving a total benefit income at their old supplementary benefit level, of whom around 19,000 claimants were in receipt of the pensioner premium and some 7,000 were disabled people aged under 60.

Special transitional additions for people with former high supplementary benefit additions for domestic assistance are uprated every year. Older and disabled pensioners on income support received a cash increase last October, through improvements to the pensioner premiums which did not erode transitional protection. In addition, increases in mobility allowance and attendance allowance are normally disregarded. As a result of these measures, about 24,000 of the claimants still on transitional protection have received some increase in their total benefit income.

section.title: Industrial Injuries
section.p: Mr. Harry Barnes: To ask the Secretary of State for Social Security if he intends to recommend changes to regulation 25(2) of the Social Security (Industrial Injuries) (Prescribed Diseases) Regulations 1985 (SI No. 967) in view of the Court of Appeal decision in the case of McKiernon v. the Secretary of State for Social Security in 1989 affecting claims for industrial deafness which are more than five years old; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Scott: No. The legality of regulation 25 of the Social Security (Industrial Injuries) (Prescribed Diseases) Regulations 1985 has been put beyond doubt by the provisions in paragraph 4(3) of schedule 6 to the Social Security Act 1990.

section.title: Social Fund
section.p: Mr. Tony Banks: To ask the Secretary of State for Social Security if he will list for each social security office in Newham the number of social fund applications (a) submitted and (b) rejected on grounds of insufficient priority since 5 April in each of the categories (i) grants, (ii) budget loans and (iii) crisis loans.
Mr. Scott: I will write to the hon. Member as soon as possible.

Mr. Cummings: To ask the Secretary of State for Social Security if he will list the number of social fund applications submitted, accepted or rejected over the last two years at the Seaham and Peterlee offices.
Mr. Scott: Details of applications processed and awards made can be obtained from information placed in the Library.

Mr. Frank Field: To ask the Secretary of State for Social Security how many and what percentage of households claiming income support are repaying social fund loans by deductions from their benefit payments.

Mr. Scott [pursuant to his reply, 24 October 1990, c. 226]: I regret that information used to calculate the percentage of income support recipients repaying social fund loans was misinterpreted. Currently 10 per cent, of income support recipients are repaying social fund loans.

section.title: Social Security Appeals
section.p: Mr. Win Griffiths: To ask the Secretary of State for Social Security how many appeals were made to the social security tribunal in 1989 and in the quarters of 1990 for which figures are available; and what is the average time appellants have had to wait for a decision in the specified periods in each standard planning region of the United Kingdom.
Mrs. Gillian Shephard: In 1989 there were 161,294 new appeals lodged with the social security appeal tribunals. I regret that similar details for the first quarter of 1990 are not yet available.
The figures show, for each of the social security regions, the average time from the date of lodgement of an appeal to the date of the tribunal hearing for the year ending 31 December 1989.

td.i: Social Security Appeal Tribunals in year ended 31 December 1989 Average number of weeks from lodgement to hearing

section.p: The figures do not include any time taken between the date of the appeal hearing and the eventual promulgation of the tribunal's decision. Responsibility for this action lies with the president of the social security and medical appeal tribunals and he has advised that a recent survey produced the following results.

td.i: Number of weeks from date of hearing to issue of decision

section.title: Mobility Allowance
section.p: Mr. Patchett: To ask the Secretary of State for Social Security how many disabled children between the ages of five and 14 years are receiving mobility allowance.
Mr. Scott: There are 18,167 such children receiving mobility allowance.

section.title: Nursing and Residential Homes, Easington
section.p: Mr. Cummings: To ask the Secretary of State for Social Security how many residents in private nursing and residential homes in the Easington constituency have been discharged because they cannot afford the charges for such accommodation.
Mrs. Gillian Shephard:This information is not available.

section.title: Disablement Benefit Gratuities
section.p: Dr. Godman: To ask the Secretary of State for Social Security if he will list by Department of Social Security office in Scotland, the number of disablement benefit gratuities paid under regulation 13 of the Social Security (Industrial Injuries and Diseases) Miscellaneous Provisions 1986.
Mr. Scott: The information could be obtained only at disproportionate cost.

section.title: Polygamous Marriages
section.p: Ms. Gordon: To ask the Secretary of State for Social Security how many pensioners in (a) London and (b) the United Kingdom have had the entitlement of their first wife to a retirement pension refused because they have entered into a second, polygamous, marriage.
Mrs. Gillian Shephard: The information requested is not available.

section.title: Disabled People
section.p: Mr. Hannam: To ask the Secretary of State for Social Security if he will take steps to monitor the impact of the community charge on disabled people.
Mr. Scott: This is a matter for my right hon. Friend the Secretary of State for the Environment.

section.title: Child Support
section.p: Sir Ian Gilmour: To ask the Secretary of State for Social Security if he will publish figures for each year since 1974–75 showing Government support for families with children, at constant April 1990 prices and in the form of indices 1974–75 = 100, and distinguishing between (a) all families with children, family allowance/child benefit, child tax allowances, non-contributory maternity benefits, (b) two-parent families, family income supplement/family credit, supplementary benefit/income support, rent and rate rebates/housing benefit, community charge benefit and (c) lone-parent families, one-parent benefit, additional personal allowance, family income supplement/family credit, supplementary benefit/income support, rent and rate rebates/housing benefit and community charge benefit.
Mrs. Gillian Shephard [holding answer 5 June 1990]: The information is not available in the form requested but the table sets out such information as is available.

Figures are as denned in the public expenditure White Papers: that is, they include child benefit, one-parent benefit, family income supplement/family credit, maternity benefits and statutory maternity pay, and supplementary benefit/income support and housing benefit payments to one-parent families. They have been supplemented by estimates of the cost of child tax allowances and additional tax allowances for lone parents in the relevant years.

section.title: Places of Entertainment (Access)
section.p: Mr. Hannam: To ask the Secretary of State for Social Security what steps he is taking to ensure that blind people and wheelchair users are not refused access to places of entertainment.
Mr. Peter Lloyd: I have been asked to reply and will write to my hon. Friend.

section.title: Developing Countries
section.p: Mrs. Clwyd: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs what is Her Majesty's Government's response to the proposal of the Italian Foreign Minister that European Community members spend 1 per cent, of gross domestic product annually to support developing countries.

Mrs. Chalker: The Italian Foreign Minister suggested in July 1990 that 1 per cent, of GDP be spent on economic assistance, with one quarter of it going to eastern Europe, one quarter to the Mediterranean countries and one half to the developing countries in general. He has not pursued the idea further with the British Government.

section.title: Pergau Hydro-electric Project
section.p: Mrs. Clwyd: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs whether the Overseas Development Administration examined a feasibility study of the Pergau hydro-electric project carried out by consultants from Snowy Mountains Co. before offering aid for the project; and what other feasibility studies and appraisal reports were examined before the decision to offer aid was made.

Mrs. Chalker: The Overseas Development Administration considered a feasibility study of this project carried out by the Snowy Mountains Engineering Corporation and mounted its own appraisal mission before making an aid offer.

section.title: Malaysia
section.p: Mrs. Clwyd: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs whether any British aid has been given or offered for road building projects in Malaysia; and if he will make a statement.

Mrs. Chalker: In 1989 the Government offered to finance a study of a proposed road building project connecting the Genting Highlands, Frasers Hill and the Cameron Highlands. This offer is still under discussion with the Malaysian authorities. Apart from this offer we have not provided or offered aid for road building projects in Malaysia in recent years.

Mrs. Clwyd: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs whether any British aid has been given or offered for gas turbine projects in Malaysia in 1989 or 1990; and if he will make a statement.

Mrs. Chalker: The Government have recently offered £23·485 million from the aid and trade provision to finance waste heat recovery units for the gas turbines at the Connaught Bridge power station. These units will increase fuel efficiency by an estimated 50 per cent. Apart from that commitment, we have not provided or offered aid for gas turbine projects in Malaysia in 1989 or 1990.

section.title: Civil Service Pensioners
section.p: Mr. Stanbrook: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs if arrangements have been made with the Government of Hong Kong for those of their pensioners who are or were expatriate members of the overseas civil service to receive credit for war service in their pensions.

Mrs. Chalker: The Hong Kong Government are still actively considering whether to include credit for war service in the calculation of pensions for those of their staff who are, or were, members of Her Majesty's overseas civil service. We were told last month that they hope to complete their deliberations by the end of this year. I will inform my hon. Friend when a decision has been made.

section.title: Licensed Teachers
section.p: Mr. Murphy: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what proportion of those individuals granted a licensed teacher award on 30 September have qualifications gained overseas.
Mr. Fallon: A total of 230 licences to teach had been granted up to 30 September 1990 of which 117 licensed teachers hold qualifications gained overseas.

Mr. Murphy: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science how many applications for the granting of a licence under the licensed teacher scheme had been received and granted by his Department on 30 June and 30 September respectively.

Mr. Fallon: Up to 30 June 1990 a total of 68 applications for a licence to teach had been received by the Department all of which were accepted and licences to teach were granted. From 1 July 1990 to 30 September a further 164 applications were received, of which 162 were accepted and licences to teach were granted.
Mr. Murphy: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what qualifications are held by those individuals granted a licensed teacher award on 30 September.
Mr. Fallon: The information is not available in the form requested.
Between 1 September 1989 and 30 September 1990, 230 licences to teach were granted, of which 187 of those licensed teachers are graduates.

Mr. Murphy: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what percentage of those individuals who have been granted the award of licensed teacher since September 1989 have an existing qualification in the secondary shortage subjects of mathematics, physics, computer and design technology and modern languages.
Mr. Fallon: The information requested is not readily available centrally.

section.title: Local Management of Schools
section.p: Mr. Jopling: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what is the average percentage of their budget distributed by shire counties for local management of schools and what is the figure for Cumbria; what is the overall education budget for Cumbria education authority; and how many schools in Cumbria are participating in local management of schools.

Mr. Fallon: The average share of the potential schools budget distributed to schools by shire counties is 77·4 per cent.; Cumbria local education authority distributes 71·2 per cent. The general schools budget of Cumbria local education authority is £149 million. All Cumbria's 361 primary and secondary schools will have control of their own budgets by April 1992.

section.title: Polytechnics
section.p: Mr. Murphy: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science if he will list the bid prices for student numbers in each programme area from each polytechnic together with the relevant Her Majesty's inspectorate's quality assessment.

Mr. Alan Howarth: This information is not held by the Department but by the Polytechnics and Colleges Funding Council. The PCFC makes it own judgments as to what information about its recurrent funding decisions should be made generally available, and what information should more appropriately remain confidential between the council and individual institutions.

section.title: Higher Education Corporations
section.p: Mr. Murphy: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science (1) how many academic and research staff, both full time and part time, are employed in each of the higher education corporations in the Polytechnics and Colleges Funding Council sector;
(2) how many academic and research staff in each of the higher education corporations are funded from sources other than the Polytechnics and Colleges Funding Council.

Mr. Alan Howarth: This information is not currently available, but will be collected by the Polytechnics and Colleges Funding Council's new staff record to be introduced for the 1991–92 academic year.

section.title: Doncaster LEA
section.p: Mr. Redmond: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science if he will list by school for the Doncaster local education authority (a) the number of teacher vacancies and (b) the subjects or speciality.
Mr. Fallon: Information on teacher vacancies by school is not held by the Department.

For Doncaster local education authority as a whole:
(a) There were 21 teacher vacancies on 18 January 1990, giving a vacancy rate of 0·8 per cent.
(b) Of these 21 vacancies, 11 were in primary schools and 10 in secondary schools. Secondary subjects with recorded vacancies were mathematics, modern languages, art, music and physical education.

section.title: Secondary School Teachers
section.p: Mr. Win Griffiths: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what is the latest information he has about the number of teachers in secondary schools who are teaching subjects for which they have (a) no degree qualification, (b) no A-level qualification and (c) no O-level qualification.

Mr. Fallon: In 1988 the proportion of tuition in maintained secondary schools in England provided by teachers who did not have a post A-level qualification in the subject taught or in a closely related one was 20 per cent. The proportion of tuition provided by teachers for whom the subject taught was not the main subject of a degree was 61 per cent. This information is taken from the 1988 secondary school staffing survey, copies of which are available in the Library.
No information is available on the A and O-level qualifications of secondary teachers.

section.title: Physical Education
section.p: Mr. Harry Greenway: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science if he has any plans to make physical education and games a compulsory part of the national curriculum; and if he will make a statement.
Mr. Fallon: Physical education, which includes games, will be a compulsory part of the curriculum in all maintained schools under the requirements of the national curriculum.

section.title: Adult Education
section.p: Mr. Bowis: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science, further to his answer to the hon. Member for Leeds, Central (Mr. Fatchett) on 12 July, Official Report, column 313, if he is now in a position to announce his decision on the future of REPLAN.
Mr. Alan Howarth: It remains my right hon. Friend's hope that a decision will be announced later this autumn.

section.title: City Technology Colleges
section.p: Mr. Grocott: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science (1) whether city technology colleges are subject to the same regulations as local education authority schools so far as requesting the submission of tenders is concerned;
(2) if he will list the rules governing the tendering procedures of city technology colleges;
(3) whether city technology colleges are subject to the European Community regulations so far as requesting submission of tenders is concerned.

Mr. Fallon: There are no specific regulations governing tenders for school buildings. The Department does however recommend that competitive tenders should be invited from a number of approved contractors. Where other methods are chosen, the Department seeks assurance that these represent good value for money. The same considerations apply to the tender process for city technology colleges, which, while subject to European Community regulations, are not governed by specific rules. In each project, the tender method used has been subject to scrutiny by the Department to ensure that effective competition has been obtained.

The number of staff employed at the Plant Breeding Institute prior to purchase of Unilever plc was 223, which included 113 in the science group.

Mr. Alan Howarth: The following information is contained in university statistics volume 1, "Students and Staff" published by the Universities' Statistical Record.

section.title: Foreign Languages
section.p: Mr. Leighton: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science if he will list the foreign languages taught in schools in England and Wales in order of popularity.

Mr. Eggar: The five modern foreign languages most commonly taught in maintained schools in England are, in order of popularity, French, German, Spanish, Italian and Russian. A number of other languages are taught to a lesser extent. Schools in Wales are a matter for my right hon. Friend the Secretary of State for Wales.

section.title: Trainee Psychologists
section.p: Mr. Steinberg: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science how many students commenced initial training as educational psychologists in September 1990; and how many of these trainees are (a) fully funded, (b) partially funded through local authority training grants and (c) self-funded.
Mr. Alan Howarth: This information is not available.

The operation of the school psychological service is a matter for the local education authorities. The Government provide specific funds to LEAs for the training of educational psychologists. In 1990–91 £2·8 million was made available which allowed all bids submitted by LEAs to be met in full.

section.title: Correspondence
section.p: Mr. Steinberg: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science what is the average time his Department takes in replying to an hon. Member's letter; and what is (a) the shortest time and (b) the longest time it has taken to reply in full to an hon. Member's letter in the last Session of Parliament.
Mr. Alan Howarth: Ministerial replies despatched in September took an average of 29 working days to issue. A
Source: SH3 return, 1979–86; SH3 and KP70 returns, 1988–89.

section.title: Elderly Mentally Ill People
section.p: Mr. Whitney: To ask the Secretary of State for Health what was the average number of residents occupying the three experimental units for elderly mentally ill people at High Wycombe, Liverpool and Hertford between 1984 and March 1990.
Mr. Dorrell: This information is not available. A total of 60 residential places were provided by the units—17 in High Wycombe, 23 in Liverpool and 20 in Hertford.
significant proportion of ministerial correspondence involves inquiries to be made of outside bodies. The rest of the information requested is not readily available.

section.title: Teacher Vacancies
section.p: Mr. Cummings: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Science if he will list, by school, in the Easington district area, the number of teacher vacancies, and the subjects or speciality.
Mr. Fallon: I shall write to the hon. Member as soon as possible.

section.title: Hospital In-patients
section.p: Mr. Redmond: To ask the Secretary of State for Health if he will list by year for the past 10 years, and by regional health authority, the number of hospital in-patients treated.
Mr. Dorrell: The information requested is given in the table.

section.title: Secondary Sensory Impairment
section.p: Mr. Cummings: To ask the Secretary of State for Health how many people in the Sunderland, Hartlepool and Durham area health authorities have been monitored, year by year, since 1985 for the development of a secondary sensory impairment.
Mr. Dorrell: This information is not held centrally.

section.title: Child Sex Abuse Cases
section.p:
Mr. Holt: To ask the Secretary of State for Health what has been the full cost to date of litigation and other legal expenses to the Northern regional health authority of the
681 Cleveland child sex abuse case and other related matters concerning the continued employment of Doctors Higgs and Wyatt.
Mr. Dorrell: The information requested is not available centrally. My hon. Friend may therefore wish to contact the chairman of Northern regional health authority.

section.title: Health Spending
section.p: Mr. Beith: To ask the Secretary of State for Health if he will show the total public expenditure on health by standard economic planning region for the latest year for which figures are available.
Mr. Dorrell: I will write to the hon. Member.

section.title: Hospital Beds
section.p: Mr. Holt: To ask the Secretary of State for Health what is the annual cost to the Northern regional health authority of a hospital bed.
Mr. Dorrell: The information requested is not available centrally. My hon. Friend may wish to contact the chairman of Northern regional health authority.

section.title: Loop System
section.p: Mr. Cummings: To ask the Secretary of State for Health if he will list the public buildings in the Easington constituency which have installed the loop system to assist the deaf and hard of hearing.
Mr. Dorrell: This information is not available centrally.

section.title: General Practitioner Lists
section.p: Mr. Patchett: To ask the Secretary of State for Health what was the average general practitioner's list size in the Barnsley health authority area in 1987, 1988, 1989 and 1990.

Mrs. Virginia Bottomley: At 1 October 1987, the average general practitioner list size in the Barnsley family health services authority's area was 2,088. The corresponding figures for 1988 and 1989 are 2,112 and 2,067. Figures for 1990 are not yet available.

section.title: Elderly People (Residential Care)
section.p: Mr. Patchett: To ask the Secretary of State for Health if he will take steps to provide for a guaranteed place in a local authority home in any case where supplementary income support for board and lodging payments to elderly people of limited or no means in private or voluntary care residential and nursing homes is inadequate or insufficient to pay the costs.

Mrs. Virginia Bottomley: Local authorities already have a duty to provide or arrange residential accommodation for elderly people in need of care and attention not otherwise available. Health authorities have similar responsibilities for people who require nursing care.

section.title: Children Act
section.p: Mr. Maxwell-Hyslop: To ask the Secretary of State for Health when local authorities will be able to obtain each of the 12 out of the total of 29 regulations pursuant to the Children Act which are still outstanding.
Mr. Dorrell: We hope to make the regulations well in advance of the implementation date of 14 October 1991.

section.title: Prescriptions
section.p: Mr. Win Griffiths: To ask the Secretary of State for Health, pursuant to the reply of 29 November 1989, Official Report, column 299, if, on the same basis, he will publish how much money was raised in prescription charges in England in 1988–89; and for what specific purposes this money, credited for class XIV, vote 2, was put.

Mr. Dorrell: Prescription charges, including receipts from the sale of pre-payment certificates, raised £176·9 million in England in 1988–89. This amount, along with other national health service charges, was used to offset the total cost of the national health service.

Mr. Harry Barnes: To ask the Secretary of State for Health if he will give the annual figures for the awarding of free prescriptions on the grounds of low income for the past three years for which figures are available.
Mrs. Virginia Bottomley: The information requested is given in the table.

section.title: Food Poisoning
section.p: Mr. Madden: To ask the Secretary of State for Health (1) what reports of people suffering Campylobacter enteritidis he has received this year, to date; how many cases of people living in Bradford have been reported; what advice he has issued to combat this disease; and if he will make a statement;
(2) what action he has taken and what advice he has issued to combat the spread of Campylobacter enteritidis; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Dorrell: The PHLS communicable disease surveillance centre has received 26,607 reports of faecal isolates of Campylobacter by laboratories in England and Wales in the first 39 weeks of this year. There have been 2,618 from the Yorkshire health region. The number from Bradford is not routinely abstracted from national surveillance data.

The advice that the Government have issued to contain the disease relates primarily to good kitchen hygiene and is contained in the publication "Food Safety: a Guide from Her Majesty's Government" copies of which are available in the Library. In May 1989 14 million copies of this food safety leaflet, jointly published by the Department of Health and the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food, were distributed to the general public.

section.title: Income Generation Unit
section.p: Mr. Harry Barnes: To ask the Secretary of State for Health what assessment he has made of the effectiveness of the work of the income generation unit; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Dorrell: The unit's role is to formulate national policy on income generation; to provide a source of advice on this for health authorities and the private sector; to 686 assist health authorities to develop and implement projects, monitor their achievements, and disseminate information and good practice.

I am pleased to report that income generation activity raised £26·8 million for the NHS in 1989–90 and it is expected that £50 million will be raised in 1990–91. The initial top target of £75 million is therefore well in sight. These substantial sums of money are making a significant contribution to improving the care offered to patients by the NHS.

section.title: Children (Employment)
section.p: Mr. Madden: To ask the Secretary of State for Health when he expects to give preliminary approval to proposed byelaws, concerning the employment of children submitted to him by Bradford council on 25 October 1989 and the subject, to date, of seven further letters; when he acknowledged receipt of the various documents; and if he will make a statement.

Mrs. Virginia Bottomley: Bradford council's draft amended byelaws have been considered by the Department; and a response was sent to the local authority on 26 October. I regret the delay; and will ensure that every effort is made to expedite approval of the byelaws.

section.title: The Gulf
section.p: Mr. Marlow: To ask the Secretary of State for Health what quantitative provision is being made for casualties from a Gulf war.

Mrs. Virginia Bottomley: I refer my hon. Friend to the reply I gave the hon. Member for Linlithgow (Mr. Dalyell) on 31 October at column 528. Should the need arise, NHS beds would be made available through restrictions on non-urgent admissions. No request for such action has yet been made by the Ministry of Defence.

section.title: Unruly Certificates
section.p: Mr. Fisher: To ask the Secretary of State for Health whether he will publish a table of all local authority social services departments showing the number of unruly certificates applied for in each department in 1989–90.
Mrs. Virginia Bottomley: This information is not collected centrally.

section.title: Public Interest Immunity Certificates

section.title: Satellite Television
section.p: Mr. Burns: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment when he will announce changes to planning controls over satellite television antennas in the light of responses to the 11 July consultation paper; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Michael Spicer: We received over 500 responses to the consultation paper. They revealed a wide divergence of views on the need for stronger controls over the siting of dishes and on the case for two dishes per house. The proposed changes to permitted development rights which we are announcing today are designed to address both these concerns: to increase the controls over installations which would damage visual amenity, especially in sensitive areas, while at the same time to ensure that the development of broadcasting services is not unduly constrained. We have also taken into account the potential use of communal systems and the likely growth of cable networks which over the next few years will contribute significantly to the further protection of the environment.

The main features of the new package being proposed by my right hon. Friend and the Secretary of State for Wales are a general provision that dishes must be sited to minimise their effect on a building's external appearance: this, combined with a new national code of practice, will give planning authorities wider power than they have at present to reduce the obtrusiveness of poorly sited dishes and will provide clearer guidance to installers on how to adopt a more consistently acceptable approach; a requirement that specific planning permission must be obtained for all installations on chimney stacks, walls and roof slopes fronting the highway in national parks, areas
693 of outstanding natural beauty and conservation areas, as well as those fronting the waterway in the Broads; a general permission for two dishes per dwellinghouse, but with stricter limits on the size of dishes; new permitted development rights for the installation of particularly small dishes on chimney stacks, where they may be less obtrusive than elsewhere on the building; new permitted development rights for installations on smaller blocks of flats, but subject to the limitations on number and size set out earlier in my reply; new permitted development rights for installations on smaller, non-domestic buildings, subject to the limitations on number and size set out above, except on chimney stacks, walls and roof-slopes fronting the highway.

We have tightened the present restrictions to take advantage of the reductions that are being achieved in the size of dishes. There will of course be further developments in antenna technology over the next few years: and by about 1995 some 65 per cent, of the population may have access to television services through underground cable networks. For these reasons we intend to review the situation again in about two years' time, to ensure that the rules take maximum advantage of technological improvements which can reduce the visual intrusiveness of dishes. I should say now that I cannot envisage any circumstances in which a general permission for more than two antennas per house would be acceptable.
To give effect to these changes, amendments to parts 1 and 25 of schedule 2 to the Town and Country Planning General Development Order 1988 will be laid before Parliament as soon as possible.

section.title: EC Treaty
section.p: Mr. Cash: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs what opinions he has sought as to the applicability of the veto (a) to amendments to the European Community treaty relating to (i) economic and monetary union or (ii) political union and (b) to any new treaty which may be proposed by member states excluding the United Kingdom as to (1) economic and monetary union and (2) political union; and if he will place any such opinion sought in the Library.

Mr. Garel-Jones: The two forthcoming intergovernmental conferences have been called to amend the treaty of Rome. Such amendments must be agreed by common accord among the member states. As my right hon. Friend the Prime Minister said in the House on 30 October, our objective in the IGCs will be to find solutions which enable the Community to go forward as Twelve.

Mr. Cash: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs what opinions he has received as to whether other member states of the European Economic Community would be in breach of their Community obligations if they sought to make a new European Community treaty for economic and monetary union or political union exclusive of the United Kingdom.

Mr. Garel-Jones: The intergovernmental conferences on economic and monetary union and political union have been called under article 236 of the treaty, which states that the conference must determine by common accord the amendments to be made to the treaty. This precludes amendment of the treaty of Rome by fewer than all member states.

section.title: Hong Kong

(b) the estimated number of Hong Kong residents eligible for naturalisation or registration as BDTCs is 1·9 million.

PO BOXNo. 1370
LONDON SW1A 2AW

section.title: Cambodia
section.p: Sir Russell Johnston: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs what discussions he has had with European Community partners about recent developments in Cambodia.

section.title: Middle East
section.p: Mr. Marlow: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs whether any commitment has been given by the United Kingdom to Israel should Iraqi forces seek to wrest the occupied territories from Israeli control.
Mr. Waldegrave: No. Such a commitment has been neither sought nor given.

Mr. Waldegrave: The Palestinian right to self-determination is not negotiable. What is for negotiation between the parties to the conflict is the shape of a comprehensive settlement of the Arab-Israel dispute.

section.title: Nuclear Non-proliferation
