Local authority houses with condensation and rising and penetrating dampness

section.title: Electoral Roll
section.p: Mr. Steinberg: To ask the Secretary of State for Scotland if he will list the number of people on the electoral roll for Scotland in 1988, 1989 and 1990.

Lord James Douglas-Hamilton: I refer the hon. Member to table 1.1 in "Electoral Statistics 1990" published by the Office of Population Censuses and Surveys—Series EL No. 17—a copy of which is in the Library.

section.title: Scottish Development Agency
section.p: Mr. Dewar: To ask the Secretary of State for Scotland how many regional directors have resigned from the Scottish Development Agency in the past two years.
Mr. Rifkind: During the period from 1 October 1988, three regional directors have resigned from the Scottish Development Agency.

Mr. McAllion: To ask the Secretary of State for Scotland (1) if he will publish in the Official Report any criteria which he required the Scottish Development Agency to satisfy before taking decisions to invest in area-based projects in Scotland;

(2) if he will publish in the Official Report the sums invested by the Scottish Development Agency in the Dundee project in each year since the project was initiated; and if he will express these figures both in terms of the actual sums invested and at 1990 prices.
Mr. Lang: I shall write to the hon. Member as soon as possible.

section.title: Hunts (Forestry Commission Land)
section.p: Mr. Ron Davies: To ask the Secretary of State for Scotland if he will take steps to ensure that hunts on Forestry Commission land are required not to fill in earths after a failed dig or at any time when an animal might still be in occupation.

Mr. Michael Forsyth: I have brought this matter to the attention of the Forestry Commission and it will be taken into account when the commission gives permission for hunting to take place on its land.

section.title: Govan Initiative
section.p: Mr. Sillars: To ask the Secretary of State for Scotland (1) what resources are available to the Govan initiative to fund the annual revenue costs for staffing and related educational costs in respect of the proposed nursery school at Merrick gardens, Ibrox;

(2) what proportion of the money Govan initiative intends to spend on the construction of a nursery school at Merrick gardens, Ibrox, comes from (a) central Government, (b) the Scottish Development Agency, (c) local government and (d) the initiative's own resources.

Mr. Lang: Approval under the urban programme was given on 9 May 1990 for a child care project which was to operate from three locations in the area of the Govan initiative. The approved costs were £279,200 in capital and £247,369 in annual running costs, initially for four years. Central Government grant would meet 75 per cent, of these costs with the balance to be provided by Strathclyde regional council. Merrick gardens was not however one of the proposed locations for this project and the Industry Department for Scotland has not been approached about any proposed change to the approved project.

section.title: Sport
section.p: Mr. Wilson: To ask the Secretary of State for Scotland (1) if he has any statistics available on teacher participation in extra-curricular sport (a) in 1980 and (b) in 1990;
(2) when he received the Scottish Sports Council's strategy documents entitled "Sport 2000"; and when he intends to respond;
(3) when he received the Scottish Sports Council's recommendation on school-age sports; and when he intends to reply;
(4) what communication there has been with the chief medical officer over the health-related aspects of the report entitled "Sports 2000", submitted to him by the Scottish Sports Council.
Mr. Michael Forsyth: I shall write to the hon. Member as soon as possible.

section.title: British Rail
section.p: Mr. Wilson: To ask the Secretary of State for Scotland if he will list the meetings which he has had with British Rail to discuss the proposed withdrawal of Speedlink freight services; and if he will make a statement.

Lord James Douglas-Hamilton: My right hon. and learned Friend met the chairman of British Rail, Sir Bob Reid, on 31 October 1990 when a number of topics were discussed including BR's present review of its Speedlink services.

Mr. Wilson: To ask the Secretary of State for Scotland if he will make a statement on his assessment of the implications for the Scottish economy and environment of the proposed withdrawal of Speedlink freight services.

Lord James Douglas-Hamilton: British Rail is currently studying the options for its Speedlink services. My right hon. and learned Friend will give consideration to the implications for Scotland of any proposals which BR puts to the Government in due course.

section.title: Mental Illness and Mental Handicap Hospitals
section.p: Mr. Win Griffiths: To ask the Secretary of State for Scotland (1) what has been the trend in admissions to mental illness hospitals and units in the last decade in the age groups for which statistics are kept;
(2) what has been the trend in admissions for mental handicap hospitals and units in the last decade in the age groups for which statistics are kept.
Mr. Michael Forsyth: I shall write to the hon. Member as soon as possible.

section.title: Foreign Languages Project
section.p: Mr. Allan Stewart: To ask the Secretary of State for Scotland when he expects replies to be sent to the letters on the foreign languages pilot project sent to the Scottish Office by Mr. and Mrs. W. Toal, 77 Rockmount avenue, Giffnock, Mr. and Mrs. J. Crawley, 113 Ayr road, Newton Mearns, Mr. and Mrs. M. Davies, 2 Tobburn avenue, Giffnock and Mr and Mrs. G. Duffy, 85 Barnfield drive, Giffnock.
Mr. Michael Forsyth: Replies were sent on 31 October.

section.title: Prescription Charges
section.p: Mr. Win Griffiths: To ask the Secretary of State for Scotland, pursuant to the reply of 29 November 1989, Official Report, column 280, if, on the same basis, he will publish how much money was raised in Scotland in prescription charges in 1988–89; and to what specific purposes this money, credited to class XVI, vote 17 subheads A2 and AZ, was put.

Mr. Michael Forsyth: The total amount raised from prescription charges in Scotland in 1988–90 was £19·565 724 million. The majority of prescription charge income was used directly to reduce the costs, borne on subhead A2 of class XVI, vote 17, of the supply of drugs and appliances prescribed or ordered by general practitioners. Other prescription charges, including those collected by dispensing doctors and those for prepayment certificates, were included in subhead AZ of class XVI, vote 17, and were used to offset total expenditure on the vote.

section.title: Fish Farming
section.p: Mr. Wilson: To ask the Secretary of State for Scotland if he will publish the findings of his Department on research into dichlorvos, and its application in fish farming.

Mr. Michael Forsyth: Scientists at the Department of Agriculture and Fisheries marine laboratory have carried out a number of studies on the effects of dichlorvos on marine species, in particular, lobster and herring larvae, mussels and invertebrates, and on the fate of dichlorvos in sea water. Reports of these studies were placed in the Library on 22 June 1990 and they have also been made available as Scottish fisheries working papers.

The Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food has also carried out surveys of farmed salmon as part of its on-going food surveillance work. Between 1987 and 1989, a total of 92 salmon samples were obtained from farms, processors and markets. No residues of dichlorvos were detected. Details of this work will be published in due course.

section.title: Community Care
section.p: Dr. Godman: To ask the Secretary of State for Scotland if he will outline the programme he intends to follow in providing additional finance to housing associations (a) in the current financial year and (b) in the 1991–92 financial year in order to ensure adequate availability of appropriate housing to match the requirements of his programme for the implementation of care in the community.

Lord James Douglas-Hamilton: Responsibility for identifying and planning for community care needs lies with social work authorities. As part of that process, social work authorities will be consulting housing associations and other voluntary housing agencies to ensure these needs are met.

My right hon. and learned Friend, through Scottish Homes, funds the overall provision for housing associations. In 1990–91 the total housing association programme is expected to be £208 million. The total for 1991–92 has not yet been determined.
It is for the housing associations themselves, in consultation with local authorities and Scottish Homes, to determine what proportion of their programme is devoted to community care.

section.title: Bottle-nosed Dolphins
section.p: Mr. Hardy: To ask the Secretary of State for Scotland whether the bottle-nosed dolphins resident in the Moray firth are now considered to be at risk.
Mr. Michael Forsyth: I shall write to the hon. Member as soon as possible.

section.title: AGR Refuellings
section.p: Mr. Dobson: To ask the Secretary of State for Scotland what percentage of refuelling is being carried out on load at each Scottish nuclear advanced gas-cooled reactor.
Mr. Lang: Questions about the operational performance of nuclear power stations in Scotland are for Scottish Nuclear Ltd.

section.title: Public Expenditure
section.p: Mr. Beith: To ask the Secretary of State for Scotland if he will show the public expenditure in Scotland on (a) agriculture, fisheries and food, (b) trade and industry, (c) employment, (d) health, (e) educational grants and (f) the administration of justice for the latest year for which figures are available.
Mr. Rifkind: I shall write to the hon. Member as soon as possible.

section.title: Local Enterprise Companies
section.p: Mr. Mc Allion: To ask the Secretary of State for Scotland if he will publish in the Official Report the names of the individuals appointed to the boards of each of the local enterprise companies in the Scottish Enterprise and Highlands and Islands Enterprise areas, indicating for each individual whether they are involved in (a) private sector business, (b) local authority, (c) a trade union, (d) other non-private sector or (e) other public sector.

Mr. Lang: At least two-thirds of the board members of local enterprise companies are to be drawn from the private sector. Individual appointments are for the local enterprise companies themselves. Board membership will be listed in the published summaries of the companies' business plans.

section.title: Self-governing Schools
section.p: Mr. Bill Walker: To ask the Secretary of State for Scotland what representations he has received concerning the future of Holm school in Orkney; if the parents will be able to vote in a second ballot at an early date if in the first ballot on self-governing status they vote narrowly to reject the option of self-governing status; and if he will make a statement.
Mr. Michael Forsyth: I shall write to my hon. Friend as soon as possible.

section.title: Carbon Emissions
section.p: Mr. Ron Davies: To ask the Secretary of State for Scotland what estimates have been made by the Forestry Commission of the potential role of woodland in absorbing carbon emissions; and if he will make a statement.
Mr. Michael Forsyth: I shall write to the hon. Member as soon as possible.

section.title: Free Television Licences
section.p: 1. Mr. Skinner: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department when he next expects to meet pensioners' representatives regarding free television licences; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Peter Lloyd: My right hon. and learned Friend is not expecting to meet pensioners' representatives about free television licences. As my right hon. and learned Friend the Member for Putney (Mr. Mellor) told the hon. Member on 6 July, we have no plans to change the present concessionary arrangements.

section.title: Sunday Trading
section.p: 2. Mr. John Marshall: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what representations he has recently received about Sunday trading.

4. Mr. Simon Coombs: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what evidence he has of progress towards finding a compromise between those who support the liberalisation of Sunday trading and those who oppose it.
31. Mr. David Evans: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what plans he has to reform the law on Sunday trading.
45. Mr. Barry Field: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what is the Government's policy on reform of the Shops Act 1950; and if he will make a statement.

Mrs. Rumbold: Since the then Home Office Minister of State, my right hon. and learned Friend the Member for Putney (Mr. Mellor), answered a similar question from my hon. Friend the Member for Hendon, South (Mr. Marshall) on 12 July at column 318, 11,321 written representations broadly in favour of Sunday trading and 18 against have been received.

It is clear that there is common ground between the interested parties on certain issues such as removing opening restrictions from small convenience stores and garden centres. We continue to encourage discussion on such matters to reach agreement in those areas where wide divisions of opinion still exist.

section.title: Car Security
section.p: 3. Mr. Anthony Coombs: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what efforts motor manufacturers have made in the last year to improve the quality of car security.

Mr. John Patten: I am aware that some motor manufacturers have taken steps to improve the quality of security in their cars, but much more remains to be done. I am currently awaiting a report from the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders on how best progress will be made in Europe towards a new mandatory common standard on car security, what plans manufacturers have for voluntarily building better security into their cars and what manufacturers are doing to encourage car buyers to give a higher priority to car security when buying a car.

section.title: Drinking Bans
section.p: 5. Mr. Devlin: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department if he will make a statement on the effectiveness of the experimental ban on drinking in public places.

Mr. John Patten: The results of the byelaw which prohibits the consumption of alcohol in designated areas
727 have been carefully monitored by the Home Office and the local authorities concerned. I am now satisfied that a byelaw of this kind can contribute to a reduction in the unpleasantness all too often associated with drinking. The effectiveness of the byelaw has been demonstrated sufficiently for it to be made generally available subject to applicant authorities satisfying themselves as to a local need and police capacity to enforce it.
16. Mr. Paice: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what steps he is taking to reduce the incidence of drunkenness on the streets.

Mr. John Patten: In addition to existing legislation, my right hon. and learned Friend the Home Secretary recently announced the general availability of the byelaw prohibiting the consumption of alcohol in certain public places to those local authorities that wish to adopt it. The byelaw is currently in operation on an experimental basis in seven selected areas and has shown that it can effectively control the nuisance of public drunkenness without becoming unduly oppressive. We are also fully supportive of the alcohol and crime demonstration projects that have been established in a number of areas.

section.title: Pornography
section.p: 6. Mr. Ieuan Wyn Jones: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department when he expects to publish the results of the review into the law relating to pornography.
Mr. John Patten: This study is a review of existing research findings from a number of countries into the behavioural and other effects of pornography. We expect to publish this review in December.

section.title: Tottenham Three
section.p: 7. Mr. Bernie Grant: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department whether he is prepared to set up an internal inquiry to look at the safety of the convictions of the Tottenham Three.

Mr. John Patten: My right hon. and learned Friend is considering very carefully a number of representations which have been made to him about the safety of the convictions of Mark Braithwaite, Engin Raghip and Winston Silcott. We will decide as soon as possible whether intervention in these cases would be justified.

section.title: Crime, North Yorkshire
section.p: 8. Mr. Gregory: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department if he will make a statement on the figures for reported crime in North Yorkshire for 1989.

Mr. John Patten: There were 35,774 offences recorded by the police in North Yorkshire during 1989. This was an increase of 3 per cent, over the previous year. Over 90 per cent, of these offences were crimes against property where effective preventive measures in support of the police by the public can help reduce the opportunities for crime.

section.title: Courthouses
section.p: 9. Mr. Amess: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department how many new courthouses have been opened in England and Wales in each of the last three years.
Mr. John Patten: Eleven new courthouses were opened during the period 1987–89—one in 1988 and 10 in 1989. In addition, four others had major improvements carried out to existing buildings.

section.title: Crime, West Yorkshire
section.p: 10. Mr. Lofthouse: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department when he will next meet the chief constable of West Yorkshire to discuss crime reduction strategies.

Mr. Peter Lloyd: My right hon. and learned Friend meets chief officers of police on a regular basis to discuss a wide range of policing matters, but he has no present plans for a meeting with the chief constable of West Yorkshire to discuss crime reduction strategies in particular.

section.title: Crime Reporting
section.p: 11. Mr. Colvin: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what is his estimate of the number of extra police officers required to keep pace with the increased work load resulting from the rise in the reporting of crimes; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Peter Lloyd: There is no simple correlation between levels of reported crime and the need for police posts. We hope to make an announcement shortly on the total number of police officers which police forces can recruit in 1991–92.

section.title: Police Shifts
section.p: 12. Mr. Evennett: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what representations he has received concerning changes to police shift working patterns.

Mr. Peter Lloyd: I am aware of suggestions which have been made from time to time that the present police regulations are unnecessarily rigid and Home Office officials have been in touch with the Association of Chief Police Officers on this matter. We shall consider further how best to make progress on the issue.

section.title: UN Drugs Convention
section.p: 13. Mr. Rathbone: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department when he expects to be in a position to ratify the 1988 United Nations drugs convention.

Mr. John Patten: We hope to ratify the convention early in the new year when all the necessary subordinate legislation under the Criminal Justice (International Co-operation) Act 1990 is brought into operation.

section.title: "Supervision and Punishment in the Community"
section.p: 14. Mrs. Maureen Hicks: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what assessment has been made of the responses to the proposals as set out in the Green Paper "Supervision and Punishment in the Community".

Mr. John Patten: We received 159 responses which are now being carefully considered. All the main probation organisations responded, as did a number of other groups and individuals. We intend to make an announcement on the way forward before the end of the year.

section.title: Right to Silence
section.p: 15. Mr. Riddick: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department if he will make a statement about his Department's plans to reform the right to silence.

28. Mr. Hind: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department if he has any proposals to change the right of silence rules for suspects interviewed by police officers; and if he will make a statement.
Mr. John Patten: We are continuing to consider what changes should be made.

section.title: Public Demonstrations
section.p: 17. Mr. Knapman: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department if he will make it his policy to require those who wish to organise large public demonstrations to (a) contribute towards the cost of the necessary police operation and (b) take out insurance against the possibility of damage caused by vandalism and public disorder.

Mr. Peter Lloyd: Recovering from organisers some or all of the costs of policing demonstrations was considered during the review of public order law which preceded the Public Order Act 1986. We concluded that it would not be possible to devise a general, workable provision. We believe that there would be similar difficulties in requiring organisers to insure against the possibility of damage caused by demonstrators.

section.title: Sentencing Policy
section.p: 18. Dr. Goodson-Wickes: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what representations he has received about sentencing policy for the guidance of magistrates courts.

Mr. John Patten: We invited comments on the White Paper "Crime, Justice and Protecting the Public" (Cm. 965) and received about 200 responses from organisations and individuals, the overwhelming majority of whom welcomed its proposals.
47. Mr. Gill: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what steps he is taking to ensure that offenders receive appropriate sentences.

Mr. John Patten: Our proposals for a coherent statutory framework for sentencing, so that the sentence reflects the seriousness of the crime, were set out in the White Paper, "Crime, Justice and Protecting the Public" (Cm. 965). We will introduce legislation to implement those proposals as soon as parliamentary time allows.

section.title: Fire Service College
section.p: 19. Mr. Flynn: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what percentage of responses expressed support for his proposal to increase direct charges for officers attending courses at the Fire Service college.

Mr. John Patten: All of the organisations which we consulted naturally wished to see the total cost of courses to continue to be met from central funds. We have gone some way towards meeting their concerns by introducing 730 direct charging in England and Wales over a period of three years. The additional costs which fall to local authorities will be taken into account when decisions are taken about the level of revenue support grant.

section.title: Police Deployment
section.p: 20. Mr. Thurnham: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what discussions he is having with chief constables about the efficient deployment of their police forces; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Peter Lloyd: Chief officers, who have operational control over the deployment of their forces, and police authorities, which are statutorily responsible for providing an adequate and efficient force in their area, are well aware of the need to ensure that police resources are deployed to best effect. The search for greater value for money is a continuing theme in all our discussions with chief officers, and of the work of Her Majesty's inspectorate of constabulary and the Home Office.

section.title: Administration of Justice
section.p: 21. Mr. Ron Brown: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what is the estimated cost for the administration of justice in England and Wales for 1990; and if he will make a statement.
Mr. John Patten: The estimated cost of the criminal justice system in England and Wales for 1989–90 is about £7 billion.

section.title: Crime, Cheshire
section.p: 22. Mr. Butler: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what measures he intends to take to reduce the level of crime in Cheshire.

Mr. John Patten: Decisions about the deployment of police resources in Cheshire are an operational matter for the chief constable. But we can all help to reduce crime by taking sensible preventive measures of the kind set out in the Government's booklet "Practical Ways to Crack Crime", and I am pleased to note that there are now over 4,000 neighbourhood watch schemes in the county, covering more than 120,000 households.

section.title: Prisons (Privatisation)
section.p: 23. Mr. Favell: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what recent representations he has received on proposals to privatise prisons.

Mrs. Rumbold: A number of those who responded to the recent discussion paper "Court escorts, Custody and Security" also referred to our plans to introduce competitive tendering for the operation of the remand centre which is under development at Everthorpe, Humberside. Their views are being considered.

section.title: Broadcasting Policy
section.p: 24. Mr. Holt: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department when he last met the chairman of the BBC to discuss broadcasting policy; and if he will make a statement.
Mr. Peter Lloyd: My right hon. and learned Friend has regular meetings with the chairman of the BBC at which a range of broadcasting issues is discussed. The last meeting was on 25 September.

section.title: Football Matches (Policing Charges)
section.p: 25. Mr. Pendry: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what measures his Department will take to monitor and regulate increases in charges for policing football matches in England and Wales.

Mr. Peter Lloyd: These charges are a matter for police authorities. We are consulting them, among others, on the terms of a Home Office circular but see no need at present for regulation or monitoring.

section.title: Women Prisoners
section.p: 26. Mrs. Heal: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what steps he is taking to reduce the number of women sentenced to prison.

Mr. John Patten: The proposals for a coherent statutory framework for sentencing set out in the White Paper "Crime, Justice and Protecting the Public" (Cm. 965) are intended to ensure that more offenders convicted of less serious, particularly property, offences are punished in the community. The national standards for community service orders, which came into effect on 1 April 1989, asked probation areas to ensure that community service placements are available for women offenders, including those who are pregnant, and offenders with young children. The new edition of "The Sentence of the Court", which reflects the Court of Appeal's guidance that custody should be used only when a court considers it absolutely necessary, refers specifically to women offenders with family responsibilities.

section.title: Crime Prevention
section.p: 27. Mr. Sheerman: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department when he will next meet the Commissioner of Police of the Metropolis to discuss crime prevention measures in the metropolis.

Mr. Peter Lloyd: The House will be aware that the commissioner suffered a heart attack on the afternoon of 29 October and is at present in St. Thomas's hospital. All hon. Members will want to wish Sir Peter a speedy recovery and offer their sympathy to Lady Imbert. While Sir Peter is indisposed, the Metropolitan police will be under the command of the deputy commissioner, Sir John Dellow, and my right hon. and learned Friend will be meeting him shortly to discuss a range of matters.

section.title: Prison Work Regimes
section.p: 29. Mr. Speller: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department in how many of Her Majesty's prisons there is a regime of hard physical outdoors work for younger, healthy inmates; and what plans he has for the extension of such regimes.

Mrs. Rumbold: Information on regime activities in individual establishments is not held centrally but a number of establishments offer opportunities for purposeful and physically demanding outside work. In 1989–90, an average of 1,500 inmates a week were employed on building maintenance and refurbishment, and at 31 March 1990, some 1,900 inmates were employed on farms and gardens activities. It is the policy of the Prison Board to enhance and develop regimes and to ensure that the facilities of prison industries and farms are used to the best effect.

section.title: Young Remand Prisoners
section.p: 30. Mr. Bellingham: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what recent representation he has received in respect of 17 and 18-year-olds being held on remand in adult prison.

Mrs. Rumbold: We have not received recent representations specifically in regard to 17 and 18-year-olds, but I am of course aware of general concern in relation to young persons remanded into custody. Our policy is that wherever possible unconvicted and unsentenced male prisoners under the age of 21 years should be held in separate units. The practical possibilities are limited by the needs of the courts and the constraints of the prison estate. The latter are being alleviated by the prison building programme and certain role changes are also under consideration.

section.title: Prisoners (Education)
section.p: 32. Mr. Harry Greenway: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department if he has any plans to give all prisoners a right of access to education; and if he will make a statement.

Mrs. Rumbold: A substantial proportion of the prison service's resources is devoted to basic education and the service aims to provide a variety of opportunities for prisoners. There was a 14 per cent, increase in student hours between 1988–89 and 1989–90.

In addition the Government are considering the recommendations of the third report from the Education, Science and Arts Committee (HC 482) on this matter, and will also wish to take into account any relevant recommendations of Lord Justice Woolf's inquiry into prison disturbances.

section.title: Private Security Companies
section.p: 33. Sir Michael McNair-Wilson: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department if he will state the terms and conditions within which private security companies offer their services.

Mr. John Patten: There are no standard terms or conditions within which private security companies offer their services. It is for individuals to decide whether there is a need for additional protection of private property or possessions, to that provided by the police and it is for individual contractees to set the terms and conditions of service required.

section.title: Prison Suicides
section.p: 34. Mr. O'Brien: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department when he will next meet Judge Tumim to discuss current levels of suicides in British prisons.

Mrs. Rumbold: Her Majesty's chief inspector of prisons, Judge Tumim, has at my right hon. and learned Friend's request been carrying out a review of the prison service's policies and procedures for preventing suicides by prison inmates in England and Wales. I understand that Judge Tumim aims to finalise his report shortly. My right hon. and learned Friend would expect to discuss the report with him.

Mr. Fisher: To ask the Secretary of Stae from the Home Department if he will list all attempted suicides in 1990 in
733 prison department establishments, stating the age, sex and status; and whether the inmate was sentenced or on remand at the time of the attempt.

Mrs. Rumbold: By 31 October, reports on 136 attempted suicides in 1990 in prison department establishments had been received at the prison service headquarters. Information on age, sex and status and whether the inmate was sentenced or on remand at the time of the attempt is not readily available and could be provided only at disproportionate cost.

section.title: Dispersal Prisons
section.p: 35. Mr. Hinchliffe: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department if he will make a statement on staffing levels in dispersal prisons.

Mrs. Rumbold: Staffing levels in each of the dispersal prisons are set to take account of the nature of the inmate population and the work to be carried out in the particular establishment. On 1 October 1990 there were 2,566 officers (including principal officers and senior officers) serving in dispersal prisons. On the same date the number of inmates in the dispersal prisons was 2,814, that is an average of 1·1 for every officer in post. The ratio of officers to inmates varies significantly between the prisons reflecting differences in their design, scale and the particular facilities which they contain.

section.title: Nationality Applications
section.p: 36. Mr. Pike: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what is the time taken to process an application for British nationality at the present time.
Mr. Peter Lloyd: In September 1990, the average time taken to complete an application for British citizenship was 23 months for registration and 32 months for naturalisation.

section.title: The Tote
section.p: 37. Mr. Alexander: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department when he intends to publish the conclusions of the Lloyds report on the privatisation of the Tote; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Peter Lloyd: As I stated in my reply to my hon. Friend on 12 July at column 328, the report by Lloyds merchant bank will not be published because it was made in confidence and contains commercially and managerially sensitive information. The report is still under consideration and the Government's conclusions will be made known in due course.

section.title: Electoral Registration
section.p: 38. Mr. Hardy: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department if he will estimate the additional costs which have been incurred in regard to the registration of electors in 1990; and to what reason he attributes this additional cost.

Mrs. Rumbold: The level of central Government grant to local authorities in respect of electoral registration increases each year to take account of inflation. There has been no other increase in the level of grant for the compilation of the 1991–92 electoral register; nor are we aware that any significant additional expenditure has been incurred by electoral registration officers this year.

section.title: Police Efficiency
section.p: 39. Mr. Nicholas Bennett: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what action is being taken to improve police efficiency.

section.title: Ethnic Monitoring
section.p: 40. Mr. Maclennan: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department if he will take steps to introduce ethnic monitoring of police, probation and court decisions as a general practice.

Mr. John Patten: Ethnic monitoring of both staff and case-load in the probation service will begin in 1991.I hope that the development of monitoring, where this is feasible and useful, together with our wide-ranging programme of research studies will provide coherent information about the treatment of members of ethnic minorities within the criminal justice system.

section.title: Strangeways Prison
section.p: 41. Mr. Roger King: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what lessons have been learned and what actions are proposed as a result of the Strangeways prison riot.
Mrs. Rumbold: We shall, of course, consider carefully the recommendations of Lord Justice Woolfs inquiry, when they are received.

A new offence of prison mutiny is to be introduced. Physical security improvements have been identified with a view to denying inmates access to roof areas and facilitating staff access and control. Arrangements for the management of incidents under the reorganised senior structure of the prison service also take account of the lessons from the April disturbances in Strangeways and elsewhere. Also those experiences are being taken into account in the development of strategies for staff training, contingency planning, the protection of vulnerable prisoners and the management of disruptive prisoners.
50. Ms. Quin: Tp ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department if he will make a statement on the dispersal of prisoners as a consequence of events in Strangeways gaol in April.

Mrs. Rumbold: Immediately before the disturbances, Her Majesty's prison Manchester held some 1,639 prisoners. It was not possible to accommodate so large a number in other prisons, and as a result substantial recourse had to be had to the use of police cells. Strenuous efforts are being made to resolve the industrial relations difficulties at a number of prisons which have since added to the problems.

As at 30 October 1990, 748 prisoners are being held in police cells who, but for the loss of prison service accommodation in Manchester, would be held in prison custody there. Twenty-one constabularies are currently involved in this operation and I am most grateful for their assistance.

section.title: Domestic Servants
section.p: 42. Mr. Archer: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department if he will estimate the number of domestic servants from overseas who, in the last 12 months, have entered the United Kingdom in company with their employers and without work permits.
Mr. Peter Lloyd: It is not possible to prepare a reliable estimate.

section.title: Refugees
section.p: 43. Mr. Madden: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what representations he has received concerning Her Majesty's Government's policy on refugees.

Mr. Peter Lloyd: We frequently receive representations on aspects of our policy towards refugees and asylum seekers from hon. Members, interested organisations and the public. That policy is rooted in our obligations under the 1951 United Nations convention relating to the status of refugees and our general determination to maintain firm and fair immigration control.

section.title: Electro-static Detection Analysis
section.p: 44. Mr. Trimble: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department whether electro-static detection analysis testing is made available as a matter of routine to the defence in all cases on indictment where the Crown relies on a written statement by the accused.

Mr. John Patten: Such analysis is not conducted routinely. The defence in preparing its case may obtain expert evidence and may seek assistance from the forensic science service. Each party is bound, under the Crown court (advance notice of expert evidence) rules 1987, to disclose to the other any expert evidence which it proposes to adduce in proceedings. In addition, under guidelines issued by the Attorney-General in 1981, the prosecution makes available to the defence any unused material if it has some bearing on the offence charged and the surrounding circumstances of the case.

section.title: Violent Crime
section.p: 46. Mr. Jack: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what assistance is available to help local police forces suddenly faced with a sharp upsurge of violent crimes.

Mr. Peter Lloyd: Government support for the police is provided in a number of ways, including an increase in 736 expenditure on the police of almost 59 per cent, in real terms since 1979, an increase in the number of police officers of over 15,300 and specific grant of 51 per cent, on police expenditure. It is the responsibility of chief officers to deploy these resources in response to violent crime or any other priority. It is clear that this is being done to good effect so that there are high clear-up rates for violent crime of which there is a lesser incidence in England and Wales than in most European countries, the United States, Canada and Australia.

section.title: Drug Seizures
section.p: 48. Mr. Vaz: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department if he will make a statement on the numbers of drug seizures in Britain in 1990.

Mr. John Patten: In the period 1 January to 23 October 1990, Customs reported a provisional total of 6,471 seizures of controlled drugs in Great Britain. The latest information in relation to seizures made by the police is for 1989, figures for which are published, along with those for seizures by Customs, in table 2.3 of the Home Office statistical bulletin issue 24/90, "Statistics of the Misuse of Drugs: Seizures and Offenders dealt with, United Kingdom 1989", a copy of which is in the Library.

section.title: Community Service Orders
section.p: 49. Mr. Jacques Arnold: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department if he will make a statement on the progress being made with community service orders.

Mr. John Patten: National standards to achieve greater consistency in the application of community service programmes were introduced on 1 April 1989; the results of the first year of operation are being analysed and should be available soon. The White Paper, "Crime, Justice and Protecting the Public", published earlier this year, outlined new proposals for community penalties, including making community service orders available with probation orders.

section.title: Border Controls
section.p: 51. Mr. Knox: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department if he will make a statement about border control between Britain and other European Community countries.

Mr. Peter Lloyd: I have nothing to add at present to the statement which my right hon. and learned Friend gave to the House on 27 June 1990 at columns 220–21, following the last meeting of Trevi and European Community Immigration Ministers in Dublin in June.

section.title: Sexual Offences
section.p: 52. Ms. Richardson: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department if he will remove the corroboration rules which exist in relation to the evidence of the victims of an alleged sexual offence; and whether he will make a statement.

Mr. John Patten: The Law Commission is reviewing the law concerning the corroboration of evidence in criminal proceedings including sexual offences. We shall consider the Law Commission's final report and any recommendations to change the law as and when they are made.

section.title: Remand
section.p: 53. Dr. Kim Howells: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what steps he is taking to reduce the numbers of people remanded in custody.

Mr. John Patten: We are promoting a range of practical measures to reduce the numbers of people remanded in custody. These include the development of more bail information schemes and an increase in the number of bail hostel places; encouragement to the courts to take measures to reduce delays; the continuing extension of custody time limits and the development of mode of trial guidelines for magistrates. We have also recently issued a circular on mentally disordered offenders which should help reduce the numbers of such people who are remanded in custody.

section.title: Custody (Boys)
section.p: Mr. Bermingham: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department how many 15 and 16-year-old boys in England and Wales were (a) remanded into penal custody and (b) sentenced to custody in 1989 and during the first six months of 1990.

Mrs. Rumbold: The readily available information is given in the table. Data for 1989 are derived from tables 2.6 and 3.10 of "Prison statistics England and Wales" (Cm. 1221), copies of which are in the Library.

td.i: Receptions1 of male juveniles into prison service establishments in England and Wales: by type of reception

tr.td: 1Excludes non-criminal prisoners. Some of the persons received in each category of prisoner were also received in another category.

section.title: Prisoners (Police Cells)
section.p: Mr. Bermingham: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department how many (a) sentenced and (b) remand prisoners were being held in police cells in England and Wales on the latest date available.

Mrs. Rumbold: On 31 October a total of 1,027 prisoners were held in police cells. It is not possible to provide a breakdown between remand and other classes of prisoners because at present these figures are not collected centrally for all police areas.

section.title: Crown Court Trials
section.p: Mr. Harry Barnes: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what information he holds on the number of cases in which defendants initially plead that they are not guilty and elect for their trials to go before a Crown court and subsequently have their cases transferred to a magistrates court; and if he will make a statement.
Mr. John Patten: Defendants do not enter a plea before electing Crown court trial and cases committed for trial there are not referred back to be tried at a magistrates court.

section.title: Prisoners (Deaths)
section.p: Mr. Bermingham: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department if he will list all deaths during 1990 of persons detained in prison department establishments, stating in each case the age and sex of the inmate, the cause of the death, the inquest verdict, the establishment where the inmate was held, whether the death occurred in the prison or in an outside hospital, whether the inmate was sentenced or on remand and whether the inmate was occupying a single cell, multi-occupied cell, on the punishment block or in the prison hospital.

Mrs. Rumbold: Almost all the information requested was given in the reply that I gave to a question from the hon. Member for Huddersfield (Mr. Sheerman) on 29 October 1990 at columns 351–54. Information about whether the inmate was occupying a single or shared cell at the time of death was not included in that reply, and is not readily available in a number of cases. I shall include this information when I write to the hon. Member for Huddersfield and send a copy of that letter to the hon. Member.

section.title: Prisoners (Local Authority Care)
section.p: Mr. Bermingham: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what percentage of male and female prisoners in England and Wales had previously been in local authority care.
Mrs. Rumbold: The information requested is not recorded centrally.

section.title: Income Support Claimants
section.p: Mr. Frank Field: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department if he will list for the latest available year the number of income support claimants sent to prison for failure to pay a court fine.

Mrs. Rumbold: While no statistics on the financial status of prisoners are recorded centrally, such information as is available suggests that perhaps three-quarters of those detained for failure to pay a court fine were in receipt of income support.

section.title: Electronic Monitoring Trials
section.p: Mr. Bermingham: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what was the average total cost of monitoring the 50 defendants placed under surveillance during the recent electronic monitoring trials in Tyneside, Nottingham and London.

Mr. John Patten: The total cost of the electronic monitoring trials was about £700,000 for 50 defendants. But the former figure includes the cost of setting up three different schemes on an experimental basis and the special production of the equipment needed. It would not be sensible to take the figure yielded by dividing the latter figure into the former as a realistic average cost for the use of electronic monitoring on a larger scale.

Mr. Bermingham: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department how many of the 50 participants in the electronic monitoring trials in England and Wales reached their trials without being brought to court for an alleged violation, breaching, being additionally charged with an offence, subsequently bailed or absconding during the monitoring period.
Mr. John Patten: I will write to the hon. Member.

section.title: Electoral Statistics
section.p: Mr. Harry Barnes: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department, pursuant to his answer to the hon. Member for Derbyshire, North-East, of 25 October, Official Report, column 258, how many names will appear on the provisional electoral register for the Finchley parliamentary constituency which is due to be published in November 1990; and how many of these are expatriate registrations.
Mrs. Rumbold: The information requested will not become available until the publication of the draft electoral register on 28 November.

section.title: Prisons (Medical Care)
section.p: Mr. Bermingham: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department how many complaints from inmates about medical care in prisons in England and Wales have been received during the last five years.

Mrs. Rumbold: Records of the type requested are not readily available and could be obtained only at disproportionate cost. However the prison service working group on grievance procedures, which published its report in July last year, produced an estimate of the proportion of complaints received at prison service headquarters which related to medical matters. That estimate produces a figure of around 1,100 medical complaints received in the last year of the old grievance procedures, which were replaced on 25 September this year.

Mr. Bermingham: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department if he will publish the findings of the research conducted by Professor Gunn into the incidence of mentally disordered inmates in the prison system in England and Wales.

Mrs. Rumbold: Professor Gunn, Institute of Psychiatry, university of London, was commissioned to produce over a three-year period a definitive statement of the dimensions of the problem of sentenced mentally disturbed offenders in the prison system in England and Wales. This is an important study which will provide a sound basis on which the Department is able to consider the further development of its policies.
The report is expected soon. Following normal practice we intend that once it has then been considered arrangements will be made for its wide dissemination.

section.title: Places of Entertainment (Access)
section.p: Mr. Hannam: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what steps he is taking to ensure that fire officers are aware of regulations on access to and egress from places of entertainment for people with disabilities.
Mr. John Patten: I will write to my hon. Friend.
Mr. Hannam: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department on what date he last published regulations and guidelines concerning access to places of entertainment for people with disabilities.
Mr. Peter Lloyd: I will write to my hon. Friend.

section.title: Neighbourhood Watch
section.p: Mr. Cummings: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department if he will make a statement concerning the neighbourhood watch schemes in the Easington district; and whether he will make extra funds available to extend the schemes.
Mr. John Patten: I will write to the hon. Member.

section.title: Remand Prisoners, Durham
section.p: Mr. Cummings: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department if he will list the number of prisoners on remand in Durham prisons in the year 1988–89, and the average length of time of such remands.
Mrs. Rumbold: I will write to the hon. Member.

section.title: Arrests
section.p: Ms. Gordon: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department, pursuant to his answer of 25 July, if he will break down the numbers of people arrested in England and Wales in 1986, 1988 and 1989 by police force areas.
Mr. Peter Lloyd: I will write to the hon. Member.

section.title: Work Permits
section.p: Mr. Tony Banks: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department (1) what action he intends to take against the BBC for employing Mr. Patrick Shai on the production of "Land of Dreams" without a work permit having been issued; and if he will make a statement;
(2) how many summonses have been issued against employers employing persons without work permits in each of the last three financial years.
Mr. Peter Lloyd: I will write to the hon. Member.

section.title: Police Officers, Peterlee
section.p: Mr. Cummings: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what was the compliment of police officers in the Peterlee subdivision for the last three years.

Mr. Peter Lloyd: The Peterlee subdivision was merged with the Seaham subdivision on 1 January 1989 to form the Easington subdivision. The table shows only that part of the establishment and strength of the Easington subdivision which covers Peterlee.

section.title: Special Constables
section.p: Mr. Patchett: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department how many special constables has South Yorkshire (a) proportionate to the population and (b) proportionate to other counties; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Waddington: South Yorkshire has an estimated population of 1,293,000 of whom 316 are members of the
741 special constabulary. Appendix 7 of the report of Her Majesty's chief inspector of constabulary lists the number of special constables and the population of force areas for each police force in England and Wales, a copy of which is available in the Library.

section.title: Labour Party Conference
section.p: Mr. Simon Hughes: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what were the total policing costs arising from the Labour party conference in Blackpool; and what proportion of the cost will be met by local authorities.

Mr. Peter Lloyd: I understand from the chief constable of Lancashire that the additional costs of policing the Labour party conference in Blackpool were £97,545. The additional costs of policing will be met by Lancashire police authority. Under the normal police funding arrangements, the Government contribute both directly through police grant—which is at 51 per cent.—and indirectly through revenue support grant.

section.title: Correspondence
section.p: Mr. Steinberg: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what is the average time his Department takes in replying to an hon. Member's letter; and what is (a) the shortest time and (b) the longest time it has taken to reply in full to an hon. Member's letter in the last Session of Parliament.
Mr. Waddington: I will write to the hon. Member.

section.title: Le Vay Report
section.p: Mr. John Evans: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department if he will make a statement on plans to implement the Le Vay report.

Mr. John Patten: We have now received and published the report of consultants appointed to prepare an assessment of the costs of implementing the main organisational recommendations in the report of the magistrates courts scrutiny 1989 and of an alternative organisational model. We are giving further thought to the scrutiny recommendations in the light of the consultants' advice and of any comments on their work by interested bodies.

section.title: Mr. Arthur Scargill
section.p: Mr. Ken Hargreaves: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department if he will call for a report from the Commissioner of Police of the Metropolis as to what permission has been sought by the company fraud department to interview Arthur Scargill, president of the National Union of Mineworkers.
Mr. Peter Lloyd: No. The police do not require permission to conduct interviews during the course of their inquiries.

Mr. Ken Hargreaves: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department if he will call for a report from the Commissioner of Police of the Metropolis as to his most up-to-date estimate of the likely completion date of the company fraud department, Metropolitan police, inquiries into the activities of Arthur Scargill, president of the National Union of Mineworkers.

Mr. Peter Lloyd: I understand from the Commissioner of Police of the Metropolis that the Metropolitan police expect their initial inquiries into the allegations against members of the NUM to be completed shortly.

section.title: London Prisons
section.p: Mr. Cox: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department if staff for new prisons are to be transferred from other London prisons; and if he will make a statement.

Mrs. Rumbold: To enable Belmarsh prison to open in April 1991, a total of 353 new prison officers will be recruited. In addition, it is proposed to redeploy to Belmarsh 202 officer posts from a number of other prisons in the London area as a consequence of the transfer of work there from those establishments. The reductions in staffing levels at existing establishments will be effected by means of wastage and voluntary transfers to other establishments.

section.title: Public Interest Immunity Certificates
section.p: Mr. Redmond: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department when and for what reasons public interest immunity certificates are issued; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Waddington: A certificate claiming public interest immunity may, exceptionally, be issued by the Secretary of State when information is sought by a party to legal proceedings relating to matters within his responsibility. It is not practicable to give a detailed description of the circumstances where such a claim would be made, but I would issue a certificate only if I was satisfied that it was necessary in the public interest to prevent disclosure of the information.

Mr. Redmond: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department if he will list by date, and by location, the number of occasions in the past 10 years when public interest immunity certificates have been issued in the three counties of Yorkshire and Humberside concerning matters before coroners and other courts preventing members of the police forces and others within the remit of his Department from attending such courts, and to prevent such courts from hearing details of operations, indicating which operations were involved and how many individuals were covered by such certificates.
Mr. Waddington: I refer the hon. Member to the reply that I gave to a question from the hon. Member for Kingston upon Hull, North (Mr. McNamara) on 17 October at column 820.

section.title: Royal Family
section.p: Mr. Redmond: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department if he will list by date and location for the last five years to date the number of intruders who have been discovered on premises (a) owned by members of the royal family and (b) where members of the royal family have been in attendance; and if he will show, in his answer, the sentences imposed by the courts.
Mr. John Patten: The information is not available in the form requested and could be obtained only at disproportionate cost.

section.title: Rape
section.p: Sir Michael McNair-Wilson: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what were the minimum sentence, the maximum sentence and the average length of sentence given in cases of rape between 1984 and 1990; and what was the average sentence served by rapists.

Mr. John Patten [holding answer 19 October 1990]: The information is not available in precisely the form requested and could be obtained only at disproportionate cost. Available statistics do not distinguish between rape, and aiding and abetting rape. The average determinate sentence for offences of rape, and aiding and abetting rape between 1984 and 1988 was as follows:
Year Average sentence length (months)
1984 44·1
1985 54·2
1986 65·5
1987 74·5
1988 74·5
In both 1984 and 1988, the maximum sentence given for rape was life imprisonment.

section.title: Earnings
section.p: Mr. Austin Mitchell: To ask the Secretary of State for Employment whether he will publish in the Official Report a table showing the increase since (a) April 1979 and (b) April 1989 in real average weekly earnings for (i) full-time adult male and (ii) full-time adult female workers, including overtime but excluding absence in the case of (w) manual workers in manufacturing, (x) other 744 manuals, (y) non-manuals and (z) journalists; and if he will provide similar figures for the period April 1974 to April 1979.

Mr. Jackson: Information on the average gross weekly earnings of full-time adult employees at April of the years in question is published in part A of the annual new earnings survey reports with the exception of manuals in non-manufacturing in the last two years, for which the figures are as follows:
Males Females
£ £
1989 207·5 131·4
1990 227·1 143·4

The available information for journalists can be found in table 8 of the reports for 1979, 1989 and 1990. Information on the retail prices index—all items—to convert the figures to 1990 prices is published in table 6.4 of Employment Gazette for April 1989 and 1990. and in table 26 of the annual supplement to Economic Trends for April of earlier years. Copies of the publications are available in the Library.

Mr. Austin Mitchell: To ask the Secretary of State for Employment whether he will publish in the Official Report a table showing the percentage increase between 1988 and 1989 in the average earnings of full-time adult male manual workers in manufacturing, including overtime and excluding absences, and the corresponding increases for (a) the whole economy and (b) non-manuals in (i) banking, finance, insurance and business services, (ii) banking and finance and (iii) education and health; and whether he will add figures for manuals employed in (c) mechanical engineering and (d) clothing, footwear and textiles.
Mr. Jackson: Information for 1988 and 1989 is published in parts A and C of the respective annual new earnings survey reports, copies of which are available in the Library.

section.title: Employment Training
section.p: Ms. Short: To ask the Secretary of State for Employment what was the number of accidents on employment training, fatal, major and minor, for each quarter since June 1989; and how many employer or project-based work placements were closed or rejected in those periods on health and safety grounds.

Mr. Jackson: Information on accidents on employment training is given in the table. Between 1 June 1989 and 30 September 1990, 11 employer or project-based work placements were closed on health and safety grounds.

Ms. Short: To ask the Secretary of State for Employment if he will give for each region and for Great Britain as a whole the number of ET trainees who have been recruited under the skill shortage category, in numbers and as a proportion of all ET recruits, for each quarter since ET began; and if he will outline what criteria were used when locally defining what is a skill shortage area of training.

Mr. Jackson: The information requested about the number and proportions of skill shortage entrants to employment can be provided only at disproportionate cost. It would not be appropriate to set national criteria for defining local skill shortage occupations.

Ms. Short: To ask the Secretary of State for Employment (1) for each region and for Great Britain as a whole, for each quarter since June 1989, what was the number of trainees on employment training who were on placements with employers or on placements in projects;

(2) if he will give for each region and for Great Britain as a whole for the latest available period the characteristics of entrants to ET showing (a) the number of male and female entrants, (b) their ethnic origins, (c) their duration of unemployment and (d) whether they had a disability.
Mr. Jackson: In view of the detailed information requested, I will write to the hon. Member as soon as possible with the information.

Ms. Short: To ask the Secretary of State for Employment what is the best estimate he has for the numbers and amounts of ET overpayments which have taken place since the start of the programme, including (a) overpayment of individual ET training allowances, numbers and amounts, (b) overpayment of grants to training agents and (c) overpayment of grants to training managers; how much has been recovered; how much has been written off; and if he will make a statement.
Mr. Jackson: I will write to the hon. Member.

section.title: Youth Training
section.p: Ms. Short: To ask the Secretary of State for Employment if he will give for each region and for Great Britain as a whole, the number of all YTS-youth training 746 trainees in training by gender, and the numbers of each sex who had contracts of employment, for each quarter since March 1988.
Mr. Jackson: The information requested could be provided only at disproportionate cost.

Ms. Short: To ask the Secretary of State for Employment if he will give for each region and for Great Britain as a whole for each month since April 1987 the (a) number of planned entrants for YTS/YT, (b) the actual number of entrants to YTS/YT and (c) the total in training in each month on YTS/YT.
Mr. Jackson: The information requested is voluminous. I will arrange for the tables to be placed in the Library.

Ms. Short: To ask the Secretary of State for Employment for each region and for Great Britain as a whole, how many YTS youth training providers there are; how many YTS/youth training providers have lost or failed to obtain approved training organisation status in each year since 1988; why ATO status has been refused or withdrawn in each case; and if he will make a statement.
Mr. Jackson: The information requested could be obtained only at disproportionate cost.

Mr. Jackson: There are currently 487 board members serving on the 36 operational training and enterprise councils (TECs). Of these, 49 are women. None of the TECs operational to date has appointed a woman as chairman.

section.p: Ms. Short: To ask the Secretary of State for Employment if he will give the output-related targets for employment training-youth training for each of the training and enterprise councils which have become operational; what proportion of each of the training and enterprise councils' budgets will be paid only if they achieve these targets; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Jackson: Output-related targets for employment training and youth training are negotiated with individual training and enterprise councils and reflect local circumstances. Generally, the agreed target has been 10 per cent, of the total TEC budget; this payment is made for the attainment of relevant vocational qualifications under youth training and jobs secured under employment training.

section.title: Back-to-Work Grant
section.p: Ms. Short: To ask the Secretary of State for Employment if he will give details of the back-to-work grant being piloted by his Department and outline what other forms of assistance are available to unemployed people who are just about to start work; and if he will make a statement.

Mr. Jackson: The Department of Employment is not piloting a back-to-work grant. Unemployed people can take advantage of the advice and help available from employment service staff. They can give information on the benefits available to people in work. These include family credit, child benefit, housing benefit and community charge benefit.

section.title: YTS Accidents
section.p: Ms. Short: To ask the Secretary of State for Employment what were the numbers of accidents on YTS—fatal, major and minor—for the periods January to March, April to June and July to September; and how many YTS placements were closed or not accepted in these periods.
Mr. Jackson: Table A gives the YTS accident figures.

tr.td: 1 Training Agency figures have been compiled on a similar basis to those prepared by the Health and Safety Executive on employed persons. However, the Training Agency's figures will include a number of accidents to trainees in educational establishments and road traffic accidents which may not have been reportable to the Health and Safety Executive had the individual been employed.
2 Major injuries are classified according to the severity criteria laid down in the Reporting of Injuries, Diseases and Dangerous Occurrences Regulations 1985.

section.p: Separate figures for closures and rejections for employer-based and project-based work placements are not kept Table B gives the reported figures of closures and rejections on health and safety grounds from 1January 1990 to 30 September 1990.

section.title: Unemployed Claimants
section.p: Ms. Short: To ask the Secretary of State for Employment if he will give the latest information showing from 9 October 1989 for each region and for Great Britain as a whole the number of unemployed claimants who have (a) been issued with warning letters for not actively seeking work, (b) had their claims referred to an adjudication officer for not actively seeking work, (c) had their claims (i) allowed or (ii) disallowed and (d) been referred to an adjudication officer for refusing suitable employment; and what is the number of those in (d) who have had their benefit disqualified.

Mr. Jackson: Questions on operational matters in the Employment Service executive agency are the responsibility of Mike Fogden, the agency's chief executive, to whom I have referred this question for reply.

section.title: Sellafield and British Nuclear Fuels
section.p: Mr. Flynn: To ask the Secretary of State for Employment (1) what studies have been commissioned by the Health and Safety Executive into radiation risks at Sellafield using the epidemiological case control method;
(2) what studies have been commissioned by Her Majesty's Government recently into the health and work records of employees of British Nuclear Fuels plc.

Mr. Forth: Following publication of the Gardner report on childhood leukaemia and lymphoma in west Cumbria, the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) has commissioned studies to examine other factors which may be relevant to Professor Gardner's findings since there appeared to be a statistical association between the incidence of childhood leukaemia and lymphoma and paternal employment at the Sellafield reprocessing plant. These studies will comprise three parts:
(a) an investigation to see if the case fathers' doses were exceptional compared with the Sellafield work force as a whole;
(b) an investigation into the occupational histories of the case fathers to see if there are any common factors; and
(c) an epidemiological case control study looking at workplace exposure and occupational histories.
The studies will proceed subject to the acceptance by the medical ethical committees of the United Kingdom of the HSE's proposals.

section.title: Employment (Over-60s)
section.p: Mr. Patchett: To ask the Secretary of State for Employment if he will publish in the Official Report statistics on the employment of over 60s in Britain; and if he will introduce legislation to protect those aged over 60 years who wish to work against prejudice from both public and private employers.

Mr. Jackson: The 1989 labour force survey found that in spring 1989 the number of people aged 60 or over in employment in Great Britain was 1,437,000. We have no plans to introduce legislation on age discrimination, since we believe that it would be difficult to apply and uncertain in its effect. Our policy is to persuade employers to consider all applicants on merit, without imposing arbitrary age limits on recruitment.

section.title: Correspondence
section.p: Mr. Steinberg: To ask the Secretary of State for Employment what is the average time his Department takes in reply to an hon. Member's letter; and what is (a) the shortest time and (b) the longest time it has taken to reply in full to an hon. Member's letter in the last Session of Parliament.
Mr. Howard: The average time taken in reply to an hon. Member's letter is 20·2 days.

Information on the shortest time and the longest time it has taken to reply in full to an hon. Member's letter in the last Session of Parliament is not readily available and could be obtained only at disproportionate cost.

section.title: Part-time and Temporary Work
section.p: Mr. Blair: To ask the Secretary of State for Employment if he will place in the Library copies of the responses received from organisations to his Department's consultation document on the European Commission's proposals on part-time and temporary work.
Mr. Forth: No. It is for the organisations which responded to decide whether to publish their views.

Mr. Blair: To ask the Secretary of State for Employment if, pursuant to his answer on 22 October,
755 Official Report, column 2, he will place in the Library a list of organisations that responded to the consultation document on part-time and temporary work.
Mr. Forth: I have arranged for the list to be placed in the Library.

section.title: Mr. Patrick Shai
section.p: Mr. Tony Banks: To ask the Secretary of State for Employment when his Department was notified by British Actors Equity Association that the BBC was employing Mr. Patrick Shai without a work permit; and what action was taken.

Mr. Forth: British Actors Equity Association wrote to my overseas labour section in this Department on 14 February 1990 saying that Mr. Patrick Shai was working. In accordance with standing instructions, this letter was forwarded on 21 February to the Home Office, which is responsible for investigating any possible breach of the Immigration Act.

section.title: Health and Safety Offences
section.p: Mr. Nigel Griffiths: To ask the Secretary of State for Employment if he will list the offences which may be committed by companies concerning the health and safety of employees, in each case specifying the notices which may be served on companies which fail to comply with statutory provisions.

Mr. Forth: The offences for which the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) and its agents are responsible are listed in sections 33(1), 36 and 37 of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974—the HSW Act—and breaches of the relevant statutory provisions, listed in schedule 1 of the HSW Act, and regulations made under them. If an inspector is of the opinion that an offence has been committed under any of this legislation, he may issue a prohibition or improvement notice in accordance with sections 21 and 22 of the HSW Act.

section.title: Atlantic Conveyor
section.p: Mr. Prescott: To ask the Secretary of State for Defence what financial contribution was made by his Department for the replacement of the Atlantic Conveyor in the Falklands war; for what purpose; and why it was not chartered to assist in the transporting of arms and forces to the Gulf military operation.

Mr. Archie Hamilton: The financial contribution made by the MOD is commercially confidential. As described in Cmnd 8758, "The Falklands Campaign: The Lessons", militarily useful features were incorporated in the vessel, involving principally a prefabricated helicopter flight deck. The vessel has not however been offered in response to our bids for sealift for the Gulf operation as other vessels more suited to the particular requirements were available for charter.

section.title: Gulf Crisis
section.p: Mr. Prescott: To ask the Secretary of State for Defence what is the cost to date of chartering Merchant Navy vessels to assist in Gulf military operations.
Mr. Archie Hamilton: It is not the Department's policy to make public how much it has paid for the charter of merchant vessels.
